metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They'll do amazing things. They spare no expense because it's a demonstration to their own people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Again, going back to the whole idea of influence, every intelligence operation that sees the light of day has two purposes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The first purpose is the intelligence operation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But if it was just the intelligence operation, it would stay secret forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The second purpose of every successful intelligence operation, when they become public, is to send a signal to the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you work against us, we will do this to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you work for us, we will take care of you in this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's a massive information campaign.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Do you think in that way, CIA is not doing a good job?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Because there's, you know, the FSB, perhaps much less so, Jerry, but the KGB did this well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Which is to send a signal, like basically communicate that this is a terrifying organization with a lot of power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So Mossad is doing a good job of that. Correct.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The psychological information warfare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And it seems like the CIA also has a lot of kind of myths about it, conspiracy theories about it, but much less so than the other agencies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: CIA does a good job of playing to the mythos.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So when General Petraeus used to be the director of CIA, 2000.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And your workout partner. I read about this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So I loved and hated those workouts with Petraeus because he is a physical beast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: He's a strong, fit, at the time, 60-something year old man.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Let me take a tangent on that because he's coming on this podcast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Oh, excellent, man.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So can you say what you've learned from the man in terms of or like what you think is interesting and powerful and inspiring about the way he sees the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Or maybe what you learned in terms of how to get strong in the gym?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Yeah, two things right away. And one of them I was going to share with you anyway.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So I'm glad that you asked the question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So the first is that on our runs and man, he runs fast and we would go for six mile runs through Bangkok.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And he talked openly about I asked him, how do you keep this mystery, this epic mythology about your fitness and your strength?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: How do you keep all of this alive with the troops?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And he had this amazing answer and he was like, I don't talk about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Myths are born not from somebody orchestrating the myth, but from the source of the myth simply being secretive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So he's like, I don't talk about it. I've never talked about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I've never exacerbated it. I just do what I do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And I let the troops talk. And he's like, when it's in favor, when it goes in favor of discipline and loyalty and commitment, I let it run.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If it starts getting destructive or damaging, then I have my my leadership team step in to fix it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But when it comes to the the mythos, the myth of him being super powered soldier, that's what he wants every soldier to be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So he lets it run. And he was fantastic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It was so enlightening when he told me when there's a myth that benefits you, you just let it go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You let it happen because it gets you further without you doing any work. It costs no investment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So the catalyst of the virality of the myth is just being mysterious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And that's what CIA does well. To go back to your first question, what does CIA do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They don't answer any questions. They don't say anything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And wherever the myth goes, the myth goes, whether it's that they sold drugs or used child prostitutes or whatever else, wherever the myth goes, they let it go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Because at the end of the day, everybody sits back and says, wow, I really just don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Now, the second thing that I learned from Petraeus, and I really am a big fan of Petraeus, I know he made personal mistakes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You don't get to be that powerful without making personal mistakes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But when I worked out with him, the one thing that my commanding officer told me not to ask about, he was like, never ask the general about his family.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I'm a family guy. So as soon as I met General Petraeus, one of the first things I asked him was,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: hey, what was it like raising a family and being the commander of forces in the Middle East?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Like you weren't with your family very much. And the thing I love about the guy, he didn't bite off my head.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: He didn't snap at me. He didn't do anything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: He openly admitted that he regretted some of the decisions that he made because he had to sacrifice his family to get there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Relationships with his children, an absentee father, missing birthdays, missing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: We all say how sad it is to miss birthdays and miss anniversaries, yada, yada, yada.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Everybody knows what that feels like. Even business people know what that feels like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The actual pain that we're talking about is when you're not there to handle your 13 year old's questions when a boy breaks up with her.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Or when you're not there to handle the bloody lip that your nine year old comes back with from their first encounter with a bully.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Those are the truly heartbreaking moments that a parent lives and dies by.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: He missed almost all of those because he was fighting a war that we forgot and we gave up on 20 years later.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: He's so honest about that. And it was really inspiring to me to be told not to ask that question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And when I broke that guidance, he didn't reprimand me. He just was authentic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And it was absolutely one of the big decisions that helped me leave CIA on my own in 2014.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And he was honest on the sacrifice you make.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The same man, the same man who just taught me a lesson about letting a myth live.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: That same guy was willing to be so authentic about this personal mistake.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I like complicated people like that. So what did you make of that calculation of family versus job?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You've given a lot of your life and passion to the CIA, to that work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You spoke positively about that world, the good it does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And yet you're also a family man and you value that. What's that calculation like? What's that trade-off like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: For me, the calculation is very clear. It's family. I left CIA because I chose my family.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: When my son was born, my wife and I found out that we were pregnant while we were still on mission.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: We were a tandem couple. My wife is also a former CIA officer, undercover like me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: We were operating together overseas. We got the positive pregnancy test like so many people do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And she cried. My wife was a badass. I was just like the accidental spy, but my wife was really good at what she does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And she cried and she was like, what do we do now? It's what we've always wanted, a child.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But we're in this thing right now. There's no space for a child.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So long story short, we had our baby. CIA brought us back to have the baby.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And when we started having the conversations about, hey, what do we do next?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Because we're not the type of people to want to just sit around and be domestic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: What do we do next? But keep in mind, we have a child now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So here's some of our suggestions. We could do this and we can do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Let us get our child to a place where we can put him into an international school or we can get him into some sort of program where we can both operate together again during the day.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But CIA just had no, they had no patience for that conversation. There was no, family is not their priority.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So the fact that we were a tandem couple, two officers, two operators trying to have a baby was irrelevant to them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So when they didn't play with us, when they did nothing to help us prioritize parenthood as part of our overall experience, that's when we knew that they never would.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And what good is it to commit yourself to a career if the career is always going to challenge the thing that you value most?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And that was the calculation that we made to leave CIA. Not everybody makes that calculation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And a big part of why I am so vocal about my time at CIA is because I am immensely appreciative of the men and women who to this day have failed marriages and poor relationships with their children because they chose national security.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They chose protecting America over their own family. And they've done it even though it's made them abuse alcohol and abuse substances and they've gotten themselves, they've got permanent diseases and issues from living and working abroad.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's just insane the sacrifice that officers make to keep America free. And I'm just not one of those people. I chose family.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You said that your wife misses it. Do you miss it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: We both miss it. We miss it for different reasons. We miss it for similar reasons, I guess, but we miss it in different ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The people, the people at CIA are just amazing. They're people that, they're everyday people like the guy in the gown next door, but so smart and so dedicated and so courageous about what they do and how they do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I mean, the sacrifices they make are massive, more massive than the sacrifices I made. So I was always inspired and impressed by the people around me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So both my wife and I absolutely miss the people. My wife misses the work because you know everything. When you're inside, it's all, I mean, we had top secret. We had TSSCI clearances at the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I had a CAT 6, CAT 12, which makes me nuclear cleared. My wife had other privy clearances that allowed her to look into, you know, areas that were specialized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But there was not, there wasn't a headline that went out that we couldn't fact check with a click of a few buttons. And she misses that because she loved that kind of problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And now you're just one of us living in the, you know, the cloud of mystery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Not really knowing anything about what's going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Exactly. But for me, I've always been the person that likes operating. And you know what you still get to do when you leave CIA? You still get to operate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Operating is just working with people. It's understanding how people think, predicting their actions, driving their direction of their thoughts, persuading them, winning negotiations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's, you still get to do that. You do that every day.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And you can apply that in all kinds of domains. Well, let me ask you on that. You were a covert CIA intelligence officer for several years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Maybe can you tell me the story of how it all began? How were you recruited? And what did the job entail to the degree you can speak about it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Feel free to direct me if I'm getting too boring or if the...

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: No, every aspect of this is super exciting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So I was leaving the United States Air Force in 2007. I was a lieutenant getting ready to pin on captain. My five years was up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And I was a very bad fit for the US Air Force. I was an Air Force Academy graduate, not by choice, but by lack of opportunity, lack of options otherwise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So I forced myself through the Academy, barely graduated with a 2.4 GPA, and then went on the Air Force taught me how to fly. And then the Air Force taught me about nuclear weapons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And I ended up as a nuclear missile commander in Montana. And I chose to leave the Air Force because I didn't like shaving my face.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I didn't like having short hair and I most definitely didn't like shining my shoes. And I did not want to be one of the people in charge of nuclear weapons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So when I found myself as a person in charge of 200 nuclear weapons, I knew that I was going down the wrong road.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I have questions about this. And more importantly, I have questions about your hair. So you had short hair at the time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Yeah, you have to. Military regulations, you can't have hair longer than one inch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Okay. And this, the beautiful hair you have now, that came to be in the CIA or after?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: This, so I discovered I had messy hair in CIA because I used to go mooch, we called it mooch. I used to go Mujahideen style, big, burly beard and crazy, wacky hair.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Because an ambiguously brown guy with a big beard and long hair can go anywhere in the world without anyone even noticing him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They either think that he's a janitor or they think that he's like some forgotten part of history, but nobody ever thinks that that guy is a spy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So it was the perfect, for me, it was one of my favorite disguises. It's what's known as a level two disguise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: One of my favorite disguises to Don was just dilapidated brown guy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Can you actually, we'll just take a million tangents. What's a level two disguise? What are the different levels of disguise? What are the disguises?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Yeah, there's three levels of disguise by and large. Level one is what we also know, what we also call light disguise. So that's essentially you put on sunglasses and a ball cap and that's a disguise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You look different than you normally look. So it's just different enough that someone who's never seen you before, someone who literally has to see you just from a picture on the internet, they may not recognize you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: That's why you see celebrities walk around with ball caps and oversized jackets and baseball hats, because they just need to not look like they look in the tabloid or not look like they look in TV.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: That's level one. Let me jump from level one to level three. Level three is all of your prosthetics, all the stuff you see in Mission Impossible, your fake ears, your fake faces, your fat suits, your stilts inside your leg, your feet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: All that's level three. Whenever they make any kind of prosthetic disguise, that's a level three disguise because prosthetics are very damning if you are caught with a prosthetic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you're caught wearing a sudden wearing a baseball hat and sunglasses, nobody's going to say you're a spy. But when you're caught with a custom made nose prosthetic that changes the way your face looks or when someone pops out a fake jaw

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: and they see that your top teeth don't look like they did in this prosthetic, then all of a sudden you've got some very difficult questions to ask or to answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Level three is extremely dangerous. Level one is not dangerous. Level two is long term disguise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Level two is all the things that you can do to permanently change the way you look for a long period of time so that whether you're aggressed in the street or whether someone breaks into your hotel room or whatever, it's real.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So maybe that's maybe you get a tattoo. Maybe you cut your hair short. Maybe you grow your hair long. Maybe you go bald.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Maybe you start wearing glasses. Well, glasses are technically a prosthetic. But you can you if you have teeth pulled, if you gain 20 pounds, really gain 20 pounds or lose 15 pounds, whatever you might do, all of that is considered level two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's designed for a long term mission so that people believe you are who you say you are in that disguise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: A lot of that is physical characteristics. What about like, you know, what actors do, which is the method acting, the method acting, sort of developing a backstory in your own mind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And then you start, you know, pretending that you host a podcast and teach at a university and then do research and so on just so that people can believe that you're not actually an agent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: What is that part of the disguise levels or not? So, yes, disguise has to do with physical character traits. That's what a disguise is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: What you're talking about is known as a cover legend. When you go undercover, what you claim to be, who you claim to be, that's called your legend, your cover legend.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Every disguise would theoretically have its own cover legend, even if it's just to describe why you're wearing what you're wearing. It's all a cover.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So the method acting, this is a fantastic point that I don't get to make very often, so I'm glad you asked.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The difference between CIA officers in the field and method actors is that method actors try to become the character.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They try to shed all vestiges of who they really are and become the character. And that's part of what makes them so amazing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But it's also part of what like makes them mentally unstable over long periods of time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Yes. One thing is extremely surprising about human nature,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: which is funny because that's not the answer I would have said, so I'm glad that you clarified this specific question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The thing that's surprising about human nature is that human beings long in their soul.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: There's a painful longing to be with other people, and that's really surprising

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: because we all want to pretend like we're strong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: We all want to pretend like we're independent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: We all want to pretend like we are the masters of our destiny,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: but what's truly consistent in all people is this longing to commune with others like us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: My more practical answer about what I've learned to be the truth is that human nature is predictable,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: and that predictability is what gives people an incredible advantage over other people,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: but that's not the surprising piece.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Even when CIA taught me that human nature is predictable, it just made sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I was like, oh yeah, that makes sense, but what I never ever anticipated was,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: no matter where I've been in the world, no matter who I've talked to, no matter what socioeconomic bracket,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: is that longing. Man, it hurts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Loneliness sucks, and togetherness feels good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Even if you're together with someone you know isn't the right person, it still feels better than being alone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I mean, that's such a deep truth you speak to, and I could talk about that for a long time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: and I particularly also have detected that in people from all walks of life,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's there.

body.input: but that longing is still there. Even if it's an ember, it's there.

body.input: These are people who are out there doing the deed every day.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I want to bring them honor and I want to do that in a way that I get to share what they can't share and what they won't share when they leave because they will also feel the silent pressure, the pressure to the shame, the judgment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: But the truth is that I've done this now long enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The first few times that I spoke out publicly, the response to being a positive voice for what the sacrifices that people are making.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's so refreshing to be an honest voice that people don't normally hear that it's too important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: One day I'm going to be gone and my kids are going to look back on all this and they're going to see their dad trying to do the right thing for the right reasons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And even if my son or daughter ends up at CIA and even if they get ridiculed for being, oh, you're the boostamante kid, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Your dad's a total sellout, whatever it might be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I want them to know, you know, dad was doing what he could to bring honor to the organization even when he couldn't stay in the organization anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So you said when you were 27, I think you didn't know what the hell you're doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So now that you're a few years older and wiser, let me ask you to put on your wise sage hat and give advice to other 27 year olds or even younger 17, 18 year olds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They're just out of high school, maybe going to college, trying to figure out this life, this career thing that they're on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: What advice would you give them about how to have a career or how to have a life that can be proud of?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: That's a powerful question, man.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Have you figured it out yet yourself?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: No, I'm, I think I'm a man. I'm a grand total of seven days smarter than I was at 27.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's not a good average.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: There's still time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: There's still time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So for all the young people out there deciding what to do, I would just say the same thing that I would say that I do say and I will say to my own kids.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You only have one life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You only have one chance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you spend it doing what other people expect you to do, you will wake up to your regret at some point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I woke up when I was 38 years old.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: My wife in many ways is still waking up to it as she watches her grandparents pass and an older generation pass away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The folks that I've that really have a blessed life are the people who learn early on to live with their own rules, live their own way and live every day as if it's the last day.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Not necessarily to waste it by being wasteful or silly, but to recognize that today is a day to be productive and constructive for yourself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you don't want a career, today is not the day to start pursuing a career just because someone else told you to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you want to learn a language, today is a day to find a way to buy a ticket to another country and learn through immersion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: If you want a date, if you want to get married, if you want a business, today is the day to just go out and take one step.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Every day you just make one new step just like CIA recruited me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Just do the next thing. If the first step seems like it's too big, then there's probably two other steps that you can do before that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Just make constant progress, build momentum, move forward and live on your own terms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: That way you don't ever wake up to the regret.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And it'll be over before you know it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Whether you regret it or not, it's true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: What do you think is the meaning of this whole thing? What's the meaning of life?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Self-respect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: That's a fast answer. There's a story behind it if you want the story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I would love to have the story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: There's a covert training base in Alabama in the south, far south in the armpit of America where elite tier one operators go to learn human intelligence stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And there's a bar inside this base. And on the wall is just scribbles of opinions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And the question in the middle of the wall says, what's the meaning of life?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And all these elite operators over the last 25 or 30 years, they all go, they get drunk and they scribble their answer and they circle it with a Sharpie.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Love, family, America, freedom, whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And then the only thing they have to do is if they're going to write something on there, they have to connect it with something else on the wall, at least one other thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So if they write love, they can't just leave it floating there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: They have to write love in a little bubble and connect it to something else, connect it to family, whatever else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: When you look at that wall, the word self-respect is on the wall and it's got a circle around it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And then you can't see any other word because of all the things that connect to self-respect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Just dozens of people have written over, have written their words down and been drawn and scribbled over because of all the lines that connect with self-respect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: So what's the meaning of life? From my point of view, I've never seen a better answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: It's all self-respect. If you don't respect yourself, how can you do anything else?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: How can you love someone else if you don't have self-respect?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: How can you build the business you're proud of if you don't have self-respect?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: How can you raise kids? How can you make a difference? How can you pioneer anything?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: How can you just wake up and have a good day if you don't have self-respect?

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The power of the individual, that's what makes this country great.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: I have to say after traveling quite a bit in Europe and especially in a place of war,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: coming back to the United States makes me really appreciate about the better angels of this nation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: The ideals it stands for, the values it stands for.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: And I'd like to thank you for serving this nation for time and humanity for time

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: and for being brave enough and bold enough to still talk about it and to inspire others,

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: to educate others, for having many amazing conversations and for honoring me by having this conversation today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: You're an amazing human. Thanks so much for talking today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Lex, I appreciate the invite man. It was a joy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Thanks for listening to this conversation with Andrew Bustamante.

body.input: And now let me leave you with some words from Sun Tzu in the art of war.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night.

metadata.title: Podcast: Andrew Bustamante: CIA Spy | Lex Fridman Podcast #310

body.input: Thank you for listening and hope to see you next time.

body.input: It's the thing in the front of the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, exactly. And in fact, the early history of neuroscientific investigation of what this front part of the brain does is sort of funny to read because it was really World War I that started people down this road of trying to figure out what different parts of the human brain do

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: in the sense that there were a lot of people with brain damage who came back from the war with brain damage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that provided, as tragic as that was, it provided an opportunity for scientists to try to identify the functions of different brain regions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that was actually incredibly productive. But one of the frustrations that neuropsychologists faced was they couldn't really identify exactly what the deficit was that arose from damage to these most kind of frontal parts of the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It was just a very difficult thing to pin down. There were a couple of neuropsychologists who identified through a large amount of clinical experience and close observation, they started to put their finger on a syndrome that was associated with frontal damage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Actually, one of them was a Russian neuropsychologist named Luria, who students of cognitive psychology still read. And what he started to figure out was that the frontal cortex was somehow involved in flexibility, in guiding behaviors that required someone to override a habit

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: or to do something unusual or to change what they were doing in a very flexible way from one moment to another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So focused on like new experiences. So the way your brain processes and acts in new experiences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, what later helped bring this function into better focus was a distinction between controlled and automatic behavior or to in other literatures, this is referred to as habitual behavior versus goal directed behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So it's very, very clear that the human brain has pathways that are dedicated to habits, to things that you do all the time, and they need to be automatized so that they don't require you to concentrate too much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So that leaves your cognitive capacity free to do other things. Just think about the difference between driving when you're learning to drive versus driving after you're fairly expert.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are brain pathways that slowly absorb those frequently performed behaviors so that they can be habits, so that they can be automatic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So that's kind of like the purest form of learning, I guess, is happening there, which is why, I mean, this is kind of jumping ahead, which is why that perhaps is the most useful for us to focusing on and trying to see how artificial intelligence systems can learn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Is that the way you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's interesting. I do think about this distinction between controlled and automatic or goal directed and habitual behavior a lot in thinking about where we are in AI research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But just to finish the kind of dissertation here, the role of the prefrontal cortex is generally understood these days sort of in contradistinction to that habitual domain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: In other words, the prefrontal cortex is what helps you override those habits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's what allows you to say, well, what I usually do in this situation is X, but given the context, I probably should do Y.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I mean, the elbow bump is a great example, right? Reaching out and shaking hands is probably habitual behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And it's the prefrontal cortex that allows us to bear in mind that there's something unusual going on right now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And in this situation, I need to not do the usual thing. The kind of behaviors that Luria reported and he built tests for detecting these kinds of things were exactly like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So in other words, when I stick out my hand, I want you instead to present your elbow. A patient with frontal damage would have a great deal of trouble with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You know, somebody proffering their hand would elicit, you know, a handshake. The prefrontal cortex is what allows us to say, hold on, hold on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's the usual thing. But I have the ability to bear in mind even very unusual contexts and to reason about what behavior is appropriate there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Just to get a sense, are us humans special in the presence of the prefrontal cortex? Do mice have a prefrontal cortex? Do other mammals that we can study?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If no, then how do they integrate new experiences?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, that's a really tricky question and a very timely question because we have revolutionary new technologies for monitoring, measuring, and also causally influencing neural behavior in mice and fruit flies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And these techniques are not fully available even for studying brain function in monkeys, let alone humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And so it's a very sort of for me, at least a very urgent question, whether the kinds of things that we want to understand about human intelligence can be pursued in these other organisms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And, you know, to put it briefly, there's disagreement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: People who study fruit flies will often tell you, hey, fruit flies are smarter than you think. And they'll point to experiments where fruit flies were able to learn new behaviors, were able to generalize from one stimulus to another in a way that suggests that they have abstractions that guide their generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I've had many conversations in which I will start by observing, you know, recounting some observation about mouse behavior where it seemed like mice were taking an awfully long time to learn a task that for a human would be profoundly trivial.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And I will conclude from that that mice really don't have the cognitive flexibility that we want to explain. And then a mouse researcher will say to me, well, you know, hold on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That experiment may not have worked because you asked a mouse to deal with stimuli and behaviors that were very unnatural for the mouse. If instead you kept the logic of the experiment the same, but put, you know, kind of put it in a, you know, presented the information in a way that aligns with what mice are used to dealing with in their natural habitats.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You might find that a mouse actually has more intelligence than you think. And then they'll go on to show you videos of mice doing things in their natural habitat, which seem strikingly intelligent, you know, dealing with, you know, physical problems, you know, I have to drag this piece of food back to my, you know, back to my lair, but there's something in my way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And how do I get rid of that thing? So I think, I think these are open questions to put it, you know, to sum that up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And then taking a small step back, related to that is you kind of mentioned we're taking a little shortcut by saying it's a geographic geographic part of the prefrontal cortex is a region of the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But if we, what's your sense in a bigger philosophical view prefrontal cortex and the brain in general, do you have a sense that it's a set of subsystems in the way we've kind of implied that are, they're pretty distinct or to what degree is it that or to what degree is it a giant interconnected mess where everything kind of does everything and it's impossible to disentangle them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think there's overwhelming evidence that there's functional differentiation, that it's clearly not the case that all parts of the brain are doing the same thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This follows immediately from the kinds of studies of brain damage that we were chatting about before. It's obvious from what you see if you stick an electrode in the brain and measure what's going on at the level of neural activity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Having said that, there are two other things to add, which kind of, I don't know, maybe tug in the other direction. One is that it's when you look carefully at functional differentiation in the brain, what you usually end up concluding, at least this is my observation of the literature, is that the differences between regions are graded rather than being discreet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It doesn't seem like it's easy to divide the brain up into true modules that have clear boundaries and that have clear channels of communication between them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This applies to the prefrontal cortex?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, the prefrontal cortex is made up of a bunch of different subregions, the functions of which are not clearly defined and the borders of which seem to be quite vague.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Then there's another thing that's popping up in very recent research, which involves application of these new techniques. There are a number of studies that suggest that parts of the brain that we would have previously thought were quite focused in their function are actually carrying signals that we wouldn't have thought would be

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: there. For example, looking in the primary visual cortex, which is classically thought of as basically the first cortical way station for processing visual information. Basically what it should care about is where are the edges in this scene that I'm viewing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It turns out that if you have enough data, you can recover information from primary visual cortex about all sorts of things like what behavior the animal is engaged in right now and how much reward is on offer in the task that it's pursuing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's clear that even regions whose function is pretty well defined at a coarse grain are nonetheless carrying some information from very different domains.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The history of neuroscience is this oscillation between the two views that you articulated, the modular view and then the big mush view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I guess we're going to end up somewhere in the middle, which is unfortunate for our understanding because there's something about our conceptual system that finds it easy to think about a modularized system and easy to think about a completely undifferentiated system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Something that lies in between is confusing, but we're going to have to get used to it, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Unless we can understand deeply the lower level mechanism of neuronal communication.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: On that topic, you kind of mentioned information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Just to get a sense, I imagine something that there's still mystery and disagreement on is how does the brain carry information and signal?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What in your sense is the basic mechanism of communication in the brain?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Well, I guess I'm old fashioned in that I consider the networks that we use in deep learning research to be a reasonable approximation to the mechanisms that carry information in the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The usual way of articulating that is to say what really matters is a rate code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What matters is how quickly is an individual neuron spiking?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What's the frequency at which it's spiking?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Is it the timing of the spike?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah. Is it firing fast or slow?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Let's put a number on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That number is enough to capture what neurons are doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's still uncertainty about whether that's an adequate description of how information is transmitted within the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are studies that suggest that the precise timing of spikes matters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are studies that suggest that there are computations that go on within the dendritic tree, within a neuron, that are quite rich and structured and that really don't equate to anything that we're doing in our artificial neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Having said that, I feel like we're getting somewhere by sticking to this high level of abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: By the way, we're talking about the electrical signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I remember reading some vague paper somewhere recently where the mechanical signal, like the vibrations or something of the neurons also communicates information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I haven't seen that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Somebody was arguing that the electrical signal, this is in the Nature paper or something like that, where the electrical signal is actually a side effect of the mechanical signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I don't think that changes the story, but it's almost an interesting idea that there could be a deeper...

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's always like in physics with quantum mechanics, there's always a deeper story that could be underlying the whole thing, but you think it's basically the rate of spiking that gets us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's like the lowest hanging fruit that can get us really far.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This is a classical view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The only way in which this stance would be controversial is in the sense that there are members of the neuroscience community who are interested in alternatives, but this is really a very mainstream view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The way that neurons communicate is that neurotransmitters arrive, they wash up on a neuron, the neuron has receptors for those transmitters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The meeting of the transmitter with these receptors changes the voltage of the neuron, and if enough voltage change occurs, then a spike occurs, one of these discrete events.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's that spike that is conducted down the axon and leads to neurotransmitter release.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This is just like neuroscience 101.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This is the way the brain is supposed to work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Now, what we do when we build artificial neural networks of the kind that are now popular in the AI community is that we don't worry about those individual spikes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We just worry about the frequency at which those spikes are being generated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: People talk about that as the activity of a neuron.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The activity of units in a deep learning system is broadly analogous to the spike rate of a neuron.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are people who believe that there are other forms of communication in the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: In fact, I've been involved in some research recently that suggests that the voltage fluctuations that occur in populations of neurons that are below the level of spike production may be important for communication.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I'm still pretty old school in the sense that I think that the things that we're building in AI research constitute reasonable models of how a brain would work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Let me ask just for fun a crazy question because I can.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Do you think it's possible we're completely wrong about the way this basic mechanism of neuronal communication, that the information is stored in some very different kind of way in the brain?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Oh, heck yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Look, I wouldn't be a scientist if I didn't think there was any chance we were wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If you look at the history of deep learning research as it's been applied to neuroscience, of course, the vast majority of deep learning research these days isn't about neuroscience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If you go back to the 1980s, there's sort of an unbroken chain of research in which a particular strategy is taken, which is, hey, let's train a deep learning system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Let's train a multilayer neural network on this task that we trained our rat on or our monkey on or this human being on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Then let's look at what the units deep in the system are doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Let's ask whether what they're doing resembles what we know about what neurons deep in the brain are doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Over and over and over and over, that strategy works in the sense that the learning algorithms that we have access to, which typically center on back propagation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: they give rise to patterns of activity, patterns of response, patterns of neuronal behavior in these artificial models that look hauntingly similar to what you see in the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Is that a coincidence?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: At a certain point, it starts looking like such coincidence is unlikely to not be deeply meaningful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, the circumstantial evidence is overwhelming.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But you're always open to a total flipping at the table.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You have co-authored several recent papers that sort of weave beautifully between the world of neuroscience and artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Maybe if we could, can we just try to dance around and talk about some of them, maybe try to pick out interesting ideas that jump to your mind from memory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So maybe looking at, we're talking about the prefrontal cortex, the 2018, I believe, paper called the Prefrontal Cortex as a Matter Reinforcement Learning System.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What is there a key idea that you can speak to from that paper?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, I mean, the key idea is about meta-learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What is meta-learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Meta-learning is by definition a situation in which you have a learning algorithm and the learning algorithm operates in such a way that it gives rise to another learning algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: In the earliest applications of this idea, you had one learning algorithm sort of adjusting the parameters on another learning algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But the case that we're interested in this paper is one where you start with just one learning algorithm and then another learning algorithm kind of emerges out of thin air.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I can say more about what I mean by that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I don't mean to be, you know, scurrent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But that's the idea of meta-learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It relates to the old idea in psychology of learning to learn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It relates to situations where you have experiences that make you better at learning something new.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Like a familiar example would be learning a foreign language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The first time you learn a foreign language, it may be quite laborious and disorienting and novel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But let's say you've learned two foreign languages.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The third foreign language obviously is going to be much easier to pick up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And why?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Because you've learned how to learn.

body.input: So we the origin of that paper was in AI work that we were doing in my group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We were we were looking at what happens when you train a recurrent neural network using standard reinforcement learning algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And and what we started to realize is that a form of meta-learning spontaneously happens in recurrent neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And and the simplest way to explain it is to say a recurrent a recurrent neural network has a kind of memory in its activation patterns.

body.input: So you have sort of loops of connectivity, which allows activity to stick around and be updated over time in psychology.
