body.input: I feel like given the burst of innovation that's happened recently on the AI side, AI is kind of ahead in the sense that there are all of these ideas that we, you know, we, you know, for which it's exciting to consider that there might be neural analogs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And neuroscience, you know, in a sense has been focusing on approaches to studying behavior that come from, you know, that are kind of derived from this earlier era of cognitive psychology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And, you know, so in some ways, fail to connect with some of the issues that we're, you know, grappling with in AI. Like, how do we deal with, you know, large, you know, complex environments?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But, you know, I think it's inevitable that this circle will keep turning and there will be a moment in the not too different, distant future when neuroscience is pelting AI researchers with insights that may change the direction of our work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Just a quick human question. Is it, you have parts of your brain, this is very meta, but they're able to both think about neuroscience and AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You know, I don't often meet people like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So do you think, let me ask a meta plasticity question. Do you think a human being can be both good at AI and neuroscience? Like what on the team at DeepMind, what kind of human can occupy these two realms?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And is that something you see everybody should be doing, can be doing, or is that a very special few can kind of jump? Just like we talk about art history, I would think it's a special person that can major in art history and also consider being a surgeon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Otherwise known as a dilettante.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: A dilettante, yeah. Easily distracted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: No.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think it does take a special kind of person to be truly world class at both AI and neuroscience, and I am not on that list.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I happen to be someone who's interested in neuroscience and psychology, involved using the kinds of modeling techniques that are now very central in AI, and that sort of, I guess, bought me a ticket to be involved in all of the amazing things that are going on in AI research right now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I do know a few people who I would consider pretty expert on both fronts, and I won't embarrass them by naming them, but there are exceptional people out there who are like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The one thing that I find is a barrier to being truly world class on both fronts is just the complexity of the technology that's involved in both disciplines now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The engineering expertise that it takes to do truly frontline, hands-on AI research is really, really considerable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The learning curve of the tools, just like the specifics of just whether it's programming or the kind of tools necessary to collect the data, to manage the data, to distribute, to compute, all that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: On the neuroscience side, there'll be all different sets of tools. Exactly, especially with the recent explosion in neuroscience methods.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Having said all that, I think the best scenario for both neuroscience and AI is to have people interacting who live at every point on this spectrum from exclusively focused on neuroscience to exclusively focused on the engineering side of AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: To have those people inhabiting a community where they're talking to people who live elsewhere on the spectrum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I may be someone who's very close to the center in the sense that I have one foot in the neuroscience world and one foot in the AI world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That central position, I will admit, prevents me, at least someone with my limited cognitive capacity, from having true technical expertise in either domain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: At the same time, I at least hope that it's worthwhile having people around who can see the connections.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The community, the emergent intelligence of the community when it's nicely distributed is useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Exactly. I've seen that work out well at DeepMind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are people who, even if you just focus on the AI work that happens at DeepMind, it's been a good thing to have some people around doing that kind of work whose PhDs are in neuroscience or psychology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Every academic discipline has its kind of blind spots and unfortunate obsessions and its metaphors and its reference points.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Having some intellectual diversity is really healthy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: People get each other unstuck, I think. I see it all the time at DeepMind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I like to think that the people who bring some neuroscience background to the table are helping with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: One of my probably the deepest passions for me, what I would say, maybe we spoke off-mic a little bit about it, but that I think is a blind spot for at least robotics and AI folks is human-robot interaction, human-agent interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Maybe, do you have thoughts about how we reduce the size of that blind spot?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Do you also share the feeling that not enough folks are studying this aspect of interaction?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Well, I'm actually pretty intensively interested in this issue now and there are people in my group who've actually pivoted pretty hard over the last few years from doing more traditional cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience to doing experimental work on human-agent interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are a couple of reasons that I'm pretty passionately interested in this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: One is it's kind of the outcome of having thought for a few years now about what we're up to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What are we doing? What is this AI research for?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What does it mean to make the world a better place? I'm pretty sure that means making life better for humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do you make life better for humans?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's a proposition that when you look at it carefully and honestly is rather horrendously complicated, especially when the AI systems that you're building are learning systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You're not programming something that you then introduce to the world and it just works as programmed like Google Maps or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We're building systems that learn from experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That typically leads to AI safety questions. How do we keep these things from getting out of control?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do we keep them from doing things that harm humans?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I hasten to say I consider those hugely important issues.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are large sectors of the research community at DeepMind and of course elsewhere who are dedicated to thinking hard all day, every day about that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I guess I would say a positive side to this too, which is to say, well, what would it mean to make human life better?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How can we imagine learning systems doing that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: In talking to my colleagues about that, we reached the initial conclusion that it's not sufficient to philosophize about that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You actually have to take into account how humans actually work and what humans want and the difficulties of knowing what humans want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The difficulties that arise when humans want different things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Human-agent interaction has become a quite intensive focus of my group lately.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: For no other reason than that, in order to really address that issue in an adequate way, psychology becomes part of the picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's a few elements there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If you focus on the robotics problem, let's say AGI, without humans in the picture, you're missing fundamentally the final step.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: When you do want to help human civilization, you eventually have to interact with humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: When you create a learning system, just as you said, that will eventually have to interact with humans, the interaction itself has to become part of the learning process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You can't just watch humans to learn about humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You have to also be part of the human world. You have to interact with humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Exactly. Then questions arise that start imperceptibly, but inevitably to slip beyond the realm of engineering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Questions like, if you have an agent that can do something that you can't do, under what conditions do you want that agent to do it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If I have a robot that can play Beethoven sonatas better than any human, in the sense that the sensitivity, the expression is just beyond what any human...

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Do I want to listen to that? Do I want to go to a concert and hear a robot play?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: These aren't engineering questions. These are questions about human preference and human culture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Psychology bordering on philosophy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Then you start asking, even if we knew the answer to that, is it our place as AI engineers to build that into these agents?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Probably the agents should interact with humans beyond the population of AI engineers and figure out what those humans want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Then when you start... I referred this a moment ago, but even that becomes complicated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What if two humans want different things and you have only one agent that's able to interact with them and try to satisfy their preferences?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Then you're into the realm of economics and social choice theory and even politics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's a sense in which if you follow what we're doing to its logical conclusion,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: then it goes beyond questions of engineering and technology and starts to shade in perceptibly into questions about what kind of society do you want?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Actually, once that dawned on me, I actually felt... I don't know what the right word is quite refreshed in my involvement in AI research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's almost like building this kind of stuff is going to lead us back to asking really fundamental questions about what's the good life and who gets to decide?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Bringing in viewpoints from multiple sub-communities to help us shape the way that we live.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It started making me feel like doing AI research in a fully responsible way could potentially lead to a kind of cultural renewal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's the way to understand human beings at the individual, at the societal level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It may become a way to answer all the silly human questions of the meaning of life and all those kinds of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Even if it doesn't give us a way of answering those questions, it may force us back to thinking about them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It might restore a certain depth or even, dare I say, spirituality to the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I don't know. Maybe that's too grandiose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Well, I'm with you. I think AI will be the philosophy of the 21st century, the way which will open the door.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think a lot of AI researchers are afraid to open that door of exploring the beautiful richness of the human-agent interaction, human-AI interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I'm really happy that somebody like you have opened that door.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: One thing I often think about is the usual schema for thinking about human-agent interaction is this dystopian, our robot overlords.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Again, I hasten to say AI safety is hugely important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I'm not saying we shouldn't be thinking about those risks. Totally on board for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Having said that, what often follows for me is the thought that there's another narrative that might be relevant,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: which is when we think of humans gaining more and more information about human life, the narrative there is usually that they gain more and more wisdom.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: They get closer to enlightenment, and they become more benevolent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The Buddha is like that's a totally different narrative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Why isn't it the case that we imagine that the AI systems that we're creating are just going to figure out more and more about the way the world works and the way that humans interact, and they'll become beneficent?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I'm not saying that will happen. I don't honestly expect that to happen without some careful setting things up very carefully, but it's another way things could go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I would even push back on that. I personally believe that the most natural human trajectories will lead us towards progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: For me, there is a sense that most trajectories in AI development will lead us into trouble.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We over-focus on the worst-case. It's like in computer science, theoretical computer science, there's been this focus on worst-case analysis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's something appealing to our human mind at some lowest level. We don't want to be eaten by the tiger, I guess.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We want to do the worst-case analysis, but the reality is that shouldn't stop us from actually building out all the other trajectories which are potentially leading to all the positive worlds, all the enlightenment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's a book, Enlightenment Now with Steven Pinker and so on. This is looking generally at human progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's so many ways that human progress can happen with AI. I think you have to do that research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You have to do that work. You have to do the not just the AI safety work of the one worst-case analysis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do we prevent that? But the actual tools and the glue and the mechanisms of human-AI interaction that would lead to all the positive interactions that can go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's a super exciting area, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We should be spending a lot of our time saying what can go wrong. I think it's harder to see that there's work to be done to bring into focus the question of what it would look like for things to go right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's not obvious. We wouldn't be doing this if we didn't have the sense there was huge potential.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We're not doing this for no reason. We have a sense that AGI would be a major boom to humanity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But I think it's worth starting now even when our technology is quite primitive asking exactly what would that mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We can start now with applications that are already going to make the world a better place like solving protein folding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think DeepMind has gotten heavy into science applications lately, which I think is a wonderful, wonderful move for us to be making.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But when we think about AGI, when we think about building fully intelligent agents that are going to be able to, in a sense, do whatever they want, we should start thinking about what do we want them to want?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What kind of world do we want to live in? That's not an easy question. I think we just need to start working on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Even on the path to, it doesn't have to be AGI, but just intelligent agents that interact with us and help us enrich our own existence on social networks, for example, on recommender systems and various intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's so much interesting interaction that's yet to be understood and studied. I mean, Twitter is struggling with this very idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do you create AI systems that increase the quality and the health of a conversation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: For sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's a beautiful, beautiful human psychology question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do you do that without deception being involved, without manipulation being involved, maximizing human autonomy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do you make these choices in a democratic way? How do we face the, again, I'm speaking for myself here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do we face the fact that it's a small group of people who have the skill set to build these kinds of systems, but what it means to make the world a better place is something that we all have to be talking about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, the world that we're trying to make a better place includes a huge variety of different kinds of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah, how do we cope with that? This is a problem that has been discussed in gory, extensive detail in social choice theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: One thing I'm really enjoying about the recent direction work has taken in some parts of my team is that we're reading the AI literature, we're reading the neuroscience literature, but we've also started reading economics and, as I mentioned, social choice theory, even some political theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: because it turns out that it all becomes relevant. It all becomes relevant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But at the same time, we've been trying not to write philosophy papers. We've been trying not to write position papers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We're trying to figure out ways of doing actual empirical research that kind of take the first small steps to thinking about what it really means for humans with all of their complexity and contradiction and paradox to be brought into contact with these AI systems in a way that really makes the world a better place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And so, the human reinforcement learning frameworks actually kind of allow you to do that machine learning. And so, that's the exciting thing about AI is it allows you to reduce the unsolvable problem, philosophical problem, into something more concrete that you can get a hold of.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And again, it allows you to kind of define the problem in some way that allows for growth in the system that's sort of, you know, you're not responsible for the details, right? You say, this is generally what I want you to do, and then learning takes care of the rest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And of course, the safety issues arise in that context, but I think also some of these positive issues arise in that context. What would it mean for an AI system to really come to understand what humans want?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And, you know, with all of the subtleties of that, right? You know, humans want help with certain things, but they don't want everything done for them, right? Part of the satisfaction that humans get from life is in accomplishing things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So, if there were devices around that did everything for, you know, I often think of the movie WALL-E, right? That's like dystopian in a totally different way. It's like, the machines are doing everything for us. That's not what we wanted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You know, anyway, I find this, you know, this opens up a whole landscape of research that feels affirmative and exciting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: To me, it's one of the most exciting and it's wide open. We have to, because it's a cool paper, talk about dopamine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Oh, yeah. Okay. So I can. We were going to, I was going to give you a quick summary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yes, a quick summary of what's the title of the paper?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think we called it a distributional code for value in dopamine-based reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So that's another project that grew out of pure AI research. A number of people at DeepMind and a few other places had started working on a new version of reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: The, which was defined by taking something in traditional reinforcement learning and just tweaking it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So the thing that they took from traditional reinforcement learning was a value signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So at the center of reinforcement learning, at least most algorithms, is some representation of how well things are going, your expected cumulative future reward.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that's usually represented as a single number. So if you imagine a gambler in a casino and the gambler is thinking,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: well, I have this probability of winning such and such an amount of money and I have this probability of losing such and such an amount of money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That situation would be represented as a single number, which is like the expected, the weighted average of all those outcomes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And this new form of reinforcement learning said, well, what if we generalize that to a distributional representation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So now we think of the gambler as literally thinking, well, there's this probability that I'll win this amount of money and there's this probability that I'll lose that amount of money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And we don't reduce that to a single number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And it had been observed through experiments, through just trying this out, that that kind of distributional representation really accelerated reinforcement learning and led to better policies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What's your intuition about? So we're talking about rewards.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So what's your intuition why that is? Why does it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Well, it's kind of a surprising historical note, at least surprised me when I learned it, that this had been tried out in a kind of heuristic way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: People thought, well, gee, what would happen if we tried? And then it had this empirically, it had this striking effect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And it was only then that people started thinking, well, gee, why, wait, why, wait, why, why is this working?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that's led to a series of studies just trying to figure out why it works, which is ongoing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But one thing that's already clear from that research is that one reason that it helps is that it drives richer representation learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So if you imagine two situations that have the same expected value, the same kind of weighted average value,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: standard deep reinforcement learning algorithms are going to take those two situations and kind of in terms of the way they're represented internally, they're going to squeeze them together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Because the thing that you're trying to represent, which is their expected value, is the same.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So all the way through the system, things are going to be mushed together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But what if those two situations actually have different value distributions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: They have the same average value, but they have different distributions of value.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: In that situation, distributional learning will maintain the distinction between these two things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So to make a long story short, distributional learning can keep things separate in the internal representation that might otherwise be conflated or squished together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And maintaining those distinctions can be useful when the system is now faced with some other task where the distinction is important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If we look at the optimistic and pessimistic dopamine neurons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So first of all, what is dopamine?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Why is this at all useful to think about in the artificial intelligence sense?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But what do we know about dopamine in the human brain?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What is it? Why is it useful? Why is it interesting?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What does it have to do with the prefrontal cortex and learning in general?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So, well, this is also a case where there's a huge amount of detail and debate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But one currently prevailing idea is that the function of this neurotransmitter dopamine resembles a particular component of standard reinforcement learning algorithms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: which is called the reward prediction error.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So I was talking a moment ago about these value representations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: How do you learn them? How do you update them based on experience?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Well, if you made some prediction about a future reward and then you get more reward than you were expecting,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: then probably retrospectively you want to go back and increase the value representation that you attached to that earlier situation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If you got less reward than you were expecting, you should probably decrement that estimate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that's the process of temporal difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Exactly. This is the central mechanism of temporal difference learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: which is one of several kind of backbone of our momentarium in NRL.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And this connection between the reward prediction error and dopamine was made in the 1990s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And there's been a huge amount of research that seems to back it up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Dopamine may be doing other things, but this is clearly, at least roughly, one of the things that it's doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But the usual idea was that dopamine was representing these reward prediction errors, again, in this kind of single number way,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: representing your surprise with a single number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And in distributional reinforcement learning, this kind of new elaboration of the standard approach,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: it's not only the value function that's represented as a single number, it's also the reward prediction error.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And so what happened was that Will Dabney, one of my collaborators,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: who was one of the first people to work on distributional temporal difference learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: talked to a guy in my group, Will Zabkirth-Nelson, who's a computational neuroscientist, and said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: gee, you know, is it possible that dopamine might be doing something like this distributional coding thing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And they started looking at what was in the literature, and then they brought me in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: We started talking to Nauchita, and we came up with some specific predictions about, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: if the brain is using this kind of distributional coding, then in the tasks that Nao has studied, you should see this, this, this, and this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that's where the paper came from. We kind of enumerated a set of predictions, all of which ended up being fairly clearly confirmed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And all of which leads to at least some initial indication that the brain might be doing something like this distributional coding,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: that dopamine might be representing surprise signals in a way that is not just collapsing everything to a single number,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: but instead is kind of respecting the variety of future outcomes, if that makes sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So, yeah, so that's showing, suggesting possibly that dopamine has a really interesting representation scheme

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: for, in the human brain, for its reward signal. Exactly. That's fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's just, that's another beautiful example of AI revealing something nice about neuroscience, potentially suggesting possibilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Well, you never know. So the minute you publish a paper like that, the next thing you think is, I hope that replicates.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Like, I hope we see that same thing in other data sets. But of course, several labs now are doing the follow-up experiments, so we'll know soon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But it has been a lot of fun for us to take these ideas from AI and kind of bring them into neuroscience and see how far we can get.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So we kind of talked about it a little bit, but where do you see the field of neuroscience and artificial intelligence heading broadly?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Like, what are the possible exciting areas that you can see breakthroughs in the next, let's get crazy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: not just three or five years, but the next 10, 20, 30 years that would make you excited and perhaps you'd be part of?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: On the neuroscience side, there's a great deal of interest now in what's going on in AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And at the same time, I feel like neuroscience, especially the part of neuroscience that's focused on circuits and systems, kind of like really mechanism focused.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's been this explosion in new technology, and up until recently, the experiments that have exploited this technology have not involved a lot of interesting behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And this is for a variety of reasons, one of which is in order to employ some of these technologies, you actually have to, if you're studying a mouse, you have to head fix the mouse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: In other words, you have to immobilize the mouse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And so it's been tricky to come up with ways of eliciting interesting behavior from a mouse that's restrained in this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But people have begun to create very interesting solutions to this, like virtual reality environments where the animal can kind of move a track ball.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And as people have kind of begun to explore what you can do with these technologies, I feel like more and more people are asking, well, let's try to bring behavior into the picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Let's try to like reintroduce behavior, which was supposed to be what this whole thing was about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And I'm hoping that those two trends, the kind of growing interest in behavior and the widespread interest in what's going on in AI, will come together to kind of open a new chapter in neuroscience research where there's a kind of a rebirth of interest in the structure of behavior and its underlying substrates.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But that research is being informed by computational mechanisms that we're coming to understand in AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: If we can do that, then we might be taking a step closer to this utopian future that we were talking about earlier, where there's really no distinction between psychology and neuroscience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Neuroscience is about studying the mechanisms that underlie whatever it is the brain is for and what is the brain for? It's for behavior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I feel like we could maybe take a step toward that now if people are motivated in the right way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You also asked about AI. So that was a neuroscience question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You said neuroscience, that's right. And especially places like DeepMind are interested in both branches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So what about the engineering of intelligence systems?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think one of the key challenges that a lot of people are seeing now in AI is to build systems that have the kind of flexibility that humans have in two senses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: One is that humans can be good at many things. They're not just expert at one thing. And they're also flexible in the sense that they can switch between things very easily and they can pick up new things very quickly because they very ably see what a new task has in common with other things that they've done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that's something that our AI systems blatantly do not have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There are some people who like to argue that deep learning and deep RL are simply wrong for getting that kind of flexibility. I don't share that belief.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But the simpler fact of the matter is we're not building things yet that do have that kind of flexibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And I think the attention of a large part of the AI community is starting to pivot to that question. How do we get that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's going to lead to a focus on abstraction. It's going to lead to a focus on what in psychology we call cognitive control, which is the ability to switch between tasks, the ability to quickly put together a program of behavior that you've never executed before, but you know makes sense for a particular set of demands.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: It's very closely related to what the prefrontal cortex does on the neuroscience side. So I think it's going to be an interesting, an interesting new chapter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So that's the reasoning side and cognition side. But let me ask the over romanticized question. Do you think we'll ever engineer an AGI system that we humans would be able to love and that would love us back?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So have that level and depth of connection?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I love that question. And it relates closely to things that I've been thinking about a lot lately, you know, in the context of this human AI research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: There's social psychology research, in particular by Susan Fisk at Princeton in the department I used to, where I used to work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Where she, she dissects human attitudes toward other humans into a sort of two dimensional, you know, a two dimensional, two dimensional scheme.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And one dimension is about ability. You know, how, how able, how capable is this other person?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And the, but the other dimension is warmth. So you can imagine another person who's very skilled and capable, but it's very cold. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And you wouldn't, you wouldn't really like highly, you might have some reservations about that other person. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: But there's also a kind of reservation that we might have about another person who, who elicits in us or displays a lot of human warmth, but is, you know, not good at getting things done. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That, that, like the greatest esteem that we, we reserve our greatest esteem really for people who are both highly capable and also quite warm. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: That's, that's like the best of the best. This is, I mean, I'm just, I'm, this isn't a normative statement I'm making. This is just an empirical, it's an empirical statement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This is what humans seem. These are the two dimensions that people seem to kind of like along which people size other people up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And, and in AI research, we really focus on this capability thing. Like we want our agents to be able to do stuff, you know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: This thing can play go at a superhuman level. That's awesome. And, but that's only one dimension.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: What's the, what about the other dimension? What would it mean for an AI system to be warm?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And, you know, I don't know, maybe there are easy solutions here. Like we can put a, put a face on our AI systems. It's cute. It has big ears.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I mean, that's probably part of it, but I think it also has to do with a pattern of behavior, a pattern of, you know, what would it mean for an AI system to display caring, compassionate behavior in a way that actually made us feel like it was for real.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah. That we didn't feel like it was simulated. We didn't feel like we were being duped.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: To me that, you know, people talk about the Turing test or some, some descendant of it. I feel like that's the ultimate Turing test.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You know, is there a, is there an AI system that can not only convince us that it knows how to reason and it knows how to interpret language, but that we're comfortable saying, yeah, that AI system is a good guy.

body.input: You know, like I mean, on the warmth scale, whatever warmth is, we kind of intuitively understand it, but we also want to be able to, to, yeah, we don't understand it explicitly enough yet to be able to engineer it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And that's, and that's an open scientific question. You kind of alluded to it several times in the human AI interaction. That's the question that should be studied and probably one of the most important questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And humans, we humans are so good at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: You know, it's not just, it's not just that we're born warm, you know, like I suppose some people are warmer than others, given, you know, whatever genes they manage to inherit, but there's also, there's also, there are also learned skills involved, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: And we learn these skills from one another. And it's not out of the question that we could build engineered systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: I think it's hopeless, as you say, that we could somehow hand design these sorts of, these sorts of behaviors, but it's not out of the question that we could build systems that kind of we, we, we, we instill in them something that sets them out in the right direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Matt Botvinick: Neuroscience, Psychology, and AI at DeepMind | Lex Fridman Podcast #106

body.input: So that they, they end up learning what it is to interact with humans in a way that's gratifying to humans. I mean, honestly, if that's not where we're headed, I want out.
