metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: state to collapse more likely this way or that way, okay? Finally, Penrose, you know, says that all

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: of this has to be true because of an argument that he makes based on Gödel's incompleteness theorem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: okay? Now, like I would say the overwhelming majority of computer scientists and mathematicians

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: who have thought about this, I don't think that Gödel's incompleteness theorem can do what he

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: needs it to do here, right? I don't think that that argument is sound, okay? But that is, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: that is sort of the tower that you have to ascend to if you're going to go where Penrose goes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And the intuition he uses with the incompleteness theorem is that basically

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: that there's important stuff that's not computable? Is that where he takes it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: It's not just that because, I mean, everyone agrees that there are problems that are

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: uncomputable, right? That's a mathematical theorem, right? But what Penrose wants to say is that, you

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: know, for example, there are statements, you know, given any formal system, you know, for doing math,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: right? There will be true statements of arithmetic that that formal system, you know, if it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: adequate for math at all, if it's consistent and so on, will not be able to prove. A famous example

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: being the statement that that system itself is consistent, right? No, you know, good formal

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: system can actually prove its own consistency. That can only be done from a stronger formal system,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: which then can't prove its own consistency and so on forever, okay? That's Gödel's theorem. But now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: why is that relevant to consciousness, right? Well, you know, I mean, the idea that it might

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: have something to do with consciousness as an old one, Gödel himself apparently thought that it did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Oh, really? That's interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, Lucas thought so, I think, in the 60s. And Penrose is really just, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: sort of updating what they and others had said. I mean, you know, the idea that Gödel's theorem

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: could have something to do with consciousness was, you know, in 1950, when Alan Turing wrote his

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: article about the Turing test, he already, you know, was writing about that as like an old and

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: well-known idea and as one that he, as a wrong one that he wanted to dispense with, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Okay, but the basic problem with this idea is, you know, Penrose wants to say that, and all of

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: his predecessors here, you know, want to say that, you know, even though, you know, this given formal

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: system cannot prove its own consistency, we as humans, sort of looking at it from the outside,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: can just somehow see its consistency, right? And the, you know, the rejoinder to that, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: from the very beginning has been, well, can we really?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I mean, maybe, you know, maybe he, Penrose can, but, you know, can the rest of us, right? And,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: you know, I noticed that, you know, I mean, it is perfectly plausible to imagine a computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: that could say, you know, it would not be limited to working within a single formal system, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: They could say, I am now going to adopt the hypothesis that this, that my formal system

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: is consistent, right? And I'm now going to see what can be done from that stronger vantage point

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: and so on. And, you know, and I'm going to add new axioms to my system. Totally plausible. There's

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: absolutely, Gödel's theorem has nothing to say against an AI that could repeatedly add new axioms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: All it says is that there is no absolute guarantee that when the AI adds new axioms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: that it will always be right. Okay? And, you know, and that's, of course, the point that

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Penrose pounces on, but the reply is obvious. And, you know, it's one that Alan Turing made 70 years

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: ago, namely, we don't have an absolute guarantee that we're right when we add a new axiom. We never

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: have. And plausibly, we never will. So on Alan Turing, you took part in the Lubner Prize?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Not really. No, I didn't. I mean, there was this kind of ridiculous claim that was made some,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: almost a decade ago about a chat bot called Eugene Goostman.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I guess you didn't participate as a judge in the Lubner Prize.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I didn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But you participated as a judge in that, I guess it was an exhibition event or something like that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: or was Eugene...

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: No, Eugene Goostman, that was just me writing a blog post because some journalists called me to

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: ask about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Did you ever chat with him?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I did chat with Eugene Goostman. I mean, it was available on the web.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Oh, interesting. I didn't know that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: So, yeah. So all that happened was that a bunch of journalists started writing

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: breathless articles about, you know, first chat bot that passes the Turing test, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And it was this thing called Eugene Goostman that was supposed to simulate a 13-year-old boy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And apparently someone had done some test where people couldn't, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: were less than perfect, let's say, distinguishing it from a human.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And they said, well, if you look at Turing's paper and you look at,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: you know, the percentages that he talked about, then, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: it seemed like we're past that threshold, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And, you know, I had a sort of, you know, different way to look at it

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: instead of the legalistic way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Like, let's just try the actual thing out and let's see what it can do with questions like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: you know, is Mount Everest bigger than a shoebox?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: OK, or just, you know, like the most obvious questions, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And then and, you know, and the answer is, well, it just kind of parries you because it doesn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: know what you're talking about, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: So just to clarify exactly in which way they're obvious,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: they're obvious in the sense that you convert the sentences into the meaning of the objects

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: they represent and then do some basic obvious, we mean, your common sense reasoning

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: with the objects that the sentences represent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Right, right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: It was not able to answer, you know, or even intelligently respond to basic common sense

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But let me say something stronger than that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: There was a famous chat pod in the 60s called Eliza, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: That, you know, that managed to actually fool, you know, a lot of people, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Or people would pour their hearts out into this Eliza because it simulated a therapist, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And most of what it would do is it would just throw back at you whatever you said, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And this turned out to be incredibly effective, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Maybe, you know, therapists know this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: This is, you know, one of their tricks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But it, you know, it really had some people convinced.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But, you know, this thing was just like, I think it was literally just a few hundred

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: lines of Lisp code, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: It was not only was it not intelligent, it wasn't especially sophisticated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: It was like a, it was a simple little hobbyist program.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And Eugene Guestman, from what I could see, was not a significant advance compared to

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Eliza, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: So, and that was really the point I was making.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And this was, you know, you didn't, in some sense, you didn't need a, like, a computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: science professor to sort of say this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Like anyone who was looking at it and who just had, you know, an ounce of sense could

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: have said the same thing, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But because, you know, these journalists were, you know, calling me, you know, like the first

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: thing I said was, well, you know, no, you know, I'm a quantum computing person.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I'm not an AI person, you know, you shouldn't ask me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But then they said, look, you can go here and you can try it out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I said, all right, all right, so I'll try it out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But now, you know, this whole discussion, I mean, it got a whole lot more interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: in just the last few months.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Yeah, I'd love to hear your thoughts about GPT-3.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And the last few months, we've had, you know, we've, the world has now seen a chat

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: engine or a text engine, I should say, called GPT-3.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: That, you know, I think it's still, you know, it does not pass a Turing test.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, there are no real claims that it passes the Turing test, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, this is how it comes out of the group at OpenAI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And, you know, they're, you know, they've been relatively careful in what they've claimed

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: about the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: But I think this, this, this, as clearly as Eugene Guestman was not in advance over Eliza,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: it is equally clear that this is a major advance over over.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Over Eliza or really over anything that the world has seen before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: This is a text engine that can come up with kind of on topic, you know, reasonable sounding

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: completions to just about anything that you ask.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You can ask it to write a poem about topic X in the style of poet Y and it will have

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: a go at that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And it will do, you know, not a great job, not an amazing job, but, you know, a passable

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: job.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, definitely, you know, as good as, you know, you know, in many cases, I would

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: say better than I would have done, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, you can ask it to write, you know, an essay, like a student essay about pretty

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: much any topic and it will get something that I am pretty sure would get at least a B minus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: you know, in the most, you know, high school or even college classes, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And, you know, in some sense, you know, the way that it did this, the way that it achieves

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: this, you know, Scott Alexander of the, you know, the much mourned blog Slate Star Codex

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: had a wonderful way of putting it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: He said that they basically just ground up the entire internet into a slurry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And, you know, to tell you the truth, I had wondered for a while why nobody had tried

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Like, why not write a chat bot by just doing deep learning over a corpus consisting of

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: the entire web, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And so now they finally have done that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And, you know, the results are very impressive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, it's not clear that, you know, people can argue about whether this is truly a step

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: toward general AI or not, but this is an amazing capability that, you know, we didn't have

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: a few years ago that, you know, if a few years ago, if you had told me that we would have

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: it now, that would have surprised me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And I think that anyone who denies that is just not engaging with what's there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: So their model, it takes a large part of the internet and compresses it in a small number

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: of parameters relative to the size of the internet and is able to, without fine tuning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: do a basic kind of a querying mechanism, just like you described where you specify a kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: of poet and then you want to write a poem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: And it somehow is able to do basically a look up on the internet of relevant things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I mean, that's what it...

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I mean, I mean, I mean...

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: How else do you explain it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: Well, okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: I mean, I mean, the training involved, you know, massive amounts of data from the internet

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: and actually took lots and lots of computer power, lots of electricity, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

body.input: You know, there are some very prosaic reasons why this wasn't done earlier, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Computational Complexity and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #130

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And now, here's my conversation with Alex Filippenko.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Let's start by talking about the biggest possible thing, the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Will the universe expand forever or collapse on itself?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, you know, that's a great question. That's one of the big questions of cosmology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And of course, we have evidence that the matter density is sufficiently low that the universe will expand forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But not only that, there's this weird repulsive effect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We call it dark energy for want of a better term.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it appears to be accelerating the expansion of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So if that continues, the universe will expand forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it need not necessarily continue. It could reverse sign, in which case the universe could, in principle, collapse at some point in the far, far future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So like in terms of investment advice, if you were to give me and then to bet all my money on one or the other, where does your intuition currently lie?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, right now, I would say that it would expand forever because I think that the dark energy is likely to be just quantum fluctuations of the vacuum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The vacuum zero energy state is not a state of zero energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That is the ground state is a state of some elevated energy which has a repulsive effect to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that will never go away because it's not something that changes with time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So if the universe is accelerating now, it will forever continue to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And yet, I mean, you so effortlessly mentioned dark energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Do we have any understanding of what the heck that thing is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, not really, but we're getting progressively better observational constraints.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So, you know, different theories of what it might be predict different sorts of behavior for the evolution of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And we've been measuring the evolution of the universe now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the data appear to agree with the predictions of a constant density vacuum energy, a zero point energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But one can't prove that that's what it is because one would have to show that the measured numbers agree with the predictions to an arbitrary number of decimal places.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And of course, even if you've got eight, nine, ten, twelve decimal places, what if in the thirteenth one, the measurements significantly differ from the prediction?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Then the dark energy isn't this vacuum state, ground state energy of the vacuum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so then it could be some sort of a field, some sort of a new energy, a little bit like light, like electromagnetism, but very different from light,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: that fills space. And that type of energy could in principle change in the distant future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It could become gravitationally attractive for all we know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There is a historical precedent to that. And that is that the inflation with which the universe began,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: when the universe was just a tiny blink of an eye old, a trillionth of a trillionth of a trillionth of a second, you know, the universe went whoosh, it exponentially expanded.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That dark energy like substance, we call it the inflaton, that which inflated the universe, later decayed into more or less normal, gravitationally attractive matter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the exponential early expansion of the universe did transition to a deceleration, which then dominated the universe for about nine billion years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And now this small amount of dark energy started causing an acceleration about five billion years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And whether that will continue or not is something that we'd like to answer, but I don't know that we will anytime soon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there could be this interesting field that we don't yet understand that's morphing over time, that's changing the way the universe is expanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, it's funny that you were thinking through this rigorously like an experimentalist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But what about like the fundamental physics of dark energy? Is there any understanding of what the heck it is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or is this the kind of the god of the gaps or the field of the gaps? So like there must be something there because of what we're observing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I'm very much a person who believes that there's always a cause. There are no miracles of a supernatural nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So, I mean, there are two broad categories. Either it's the vacuum zero point energy or it's some sort of a new energy field that pervades the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The latter could change with time. The former, the vacuum energy cannot. So if it turns out that it's one of these new fields, and there are many, many possibilities, they go by the name of quintessence and things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But there are many categories of those sorts of fields. We try with data to rule them out by comparing the actual measurements with the predictions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And some have been ruled out, but many, many others remain to be tested. And the data just have to become a lot better before we can rule out most of them and become reasonably convinced that this is a vacuum energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there is hypotheses for different fields with names and stuff like that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, generically quintessence like the Aristotelian fifth essence, but there are many, many versions of quintessence. There's K-essence. There's even ideas that this isn't something from within this dark energy, but rather there are a bunch of, say, bubble universes surrounding our universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And this whole idea of the multiverse is not some crazy madman type idea anymore. It's real card carrying physicists are seriously considering this possibility of a multiverse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And some types of multiverses could have a bunch of bubbles on the outside, which gravitationally act outward on our bubble because gravity or gravitons, the quantum particle that is thought to carry gravity, is thought to traverse the bulk,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: the space between these different little bubble membranes and stuff. And so it's conceivable that these other universes are pulling outward on us. That's not a favorite explanation right now, but really nothing has been ruled out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: No class of models has been ruled out completely. Certain examples within classes of models have been ruled out. But in general, I think we still have really a lot to learn about what's causing this observed acceleration of the expansion of the universe, be it dark energy or some forces from the outside.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or perhaps, I guess it's conceivable that, and sometimes I wake up in the middle of the night screaming, that dark energy, that which causes the acceleration, and dark matter, that which causes galaxies and clusters of galaxies to be bound gravitationally, even though there's not enough visible matter to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe these are our 20th and 21st century Ptolemaic epicycles. So Ptolemy had a geocentric and Aristotelian view of the world. Everything goes around Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But in order to explain the backward motion of planets among the stars that happens every year or two, or sometimes several times a year for Mercury and Venus, you needed the planets to go around in little circles called epicycles,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: which themselves then went around Earth. And in this part of the epicycle where the planet is going in the direction opposite to the direction of the overall epicycle, it can appear in projection to be going backward among the stars, so-called retrograde motion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it was a brilliant mathematical scheme. In fact, he could have added epicycles on top of epicycles and reproduce the observed positions of planets to arbitrary accuracy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And this is really the beginning of what we now call Fourier analysis. Any periodic function can be represented by a sum of sines and cosines of different periods, amplitudes, and phases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it could have worked arbitrarily well. But other data show that, in fact, Earth is going around the Sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So are dark energy and dark matter just these band-aids that we now have to try to explain the data, but they're just completely wrong? That's a possibility as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And as a scientist, I have to be open to that possibility as an open-minded scientist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: How do you put yourself in the mindset of somebody that, or majority of the scientific community or majority of people believe that the Earth, everything rotates around Earth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: how do you put yourself in that mindset and then take a leap to propose a model that the Sun is, in fact, at the center of the solar system?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure. So that puts us back in the shoes of Copernicus 500 years ago, where he had this philosophical preference for the Sun being the dominant body in what we now call the solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The observational evidence in terms of the measured positions of planets was not better explained by the heliocentric Sun-centered system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's just that Copernicus saw that the Sun is the source of all our light and heat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh, wow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And he knew from other studies that it's far away. So the fact that it appears as big as the Moon means it's actually way, way bigger, because even at that time it was known that the Sun is much farther away than the Moon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So he just felt, wow, it's big, it's bright. What if it's the central thing? But the observed positions of planets at the time in the early to mid 16th century under the heliocentric system was not a better match, at least not a significantly better match than Ptolemy's system, which was quite accurate and lasted 1500 years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's so fascinating to think that the philosophical predispositions that you bring to the table are essential.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So like you have to have a young person come along that has a weird infatuation with the Sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That almost philosophically is like however their upbringing is, they're more ready for whatever the more, the simpler answer is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh, that's kind of sad. It's sad from an individual descendant of a perspective because then that means like me, like you as a scientist, you're stuck with whatever the heck philosophies you brought to the table. You might be almost completely unable to think outside this particular box you've built.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. This is why I'm saying that as an objective scientist, one needs to have an open mind to crazy sounding new ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And even Copernicus was very much a man of his time and dedicated his work to the Pope. He still used circular orbits. The Sun was a little bit off center, it turns out, and a slightly off center circle looks like a slightly eccentric elliptical orbit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So then when Kepler in fact showed that the orbits are actually in general ellipses, not circles, the reason that he needed to co-bra has really great data to show that distinction was that a slightly off center circle is not much different from a slightly eccentric ellipse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so there wasn't much difference between Kepler's view and Copernicus's view and Kepler needed the better data to co-bra's data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so that's again, a great example of science and observations and experiments working together with hypotheses and they kind of bounce off each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They play off of each other and you continually need more observations. And it wasn't until Galileo's work around 1610 that actual evidence for the heliocentric hypothesis emerged.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It came in the form of Venus, the planet Venus, going through all of the possible phases from new to crescent to quarter to gibbous to full to waning gibbous third quarter waning crescent and then new again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It turns out in the Ptolemaic system with Venus between Earth and the sun, but always roughly in the direction of the sun, you could only get the new and crescent phases of Venus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the observation showed a full set of phases and moreover when Venus was gibbous or full, that meant it was on the far side of the sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That meant it was farther from Earth than when it's crescent, so it should appear smaller and indeed it did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that was the nail in the coffin in a sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then Galileo's other great observation was that Jupiter has moons going around it, the four Galilean satellites.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And even though Jupiter moves through space, so too do the moons go with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So first of all, Earth is not the only thing that has other things going around it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And secondly, Earth could be moving as Jupiter does and things would move with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We wouldn't fly off the surface and our moon wouldn't be left behind and all this kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that was a big breakthrough as well, but it wasn't as definitive in my opinion as the phases of Venus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Perhaps I'm revealing my ignorance, but I didn't realize how much data they were working with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it wasn't Einstein or Freud thinking in theories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It was a lot of data and you're playing with it and seeing how to make sense of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it isn't just coming up with completely abstract thought experiments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's looking at the data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure, and you look at Newton's great work, the Principia.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It was based in part on Galileo's observations of balls rolling down inclined planes, supposedly falling off the Leaning Tower of Pisa, but that's probably apocryphal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In any case, the Inquisition or the Roman Catholic Church did history a favor, not that I'm condoning them, but they placed Galileo under house arrest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that gave Galileo time to assemble and publish the results of his experiments that he had done decades earlier.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's not clear he would have had time to do that had he not been under house arrest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so Newton, of course, very much used Galileo's observations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Let me ask the old Russian overly philosophical question about death.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So we're talking about the expanding universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: How do you think human civilization will come to an end if we avoid the near term issues we're having?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Will it be our sun burning out?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Will it be comets?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Will it be, what is it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Do you think we have a shot at reaching the heat death of the universe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So we're going to leave out the anthropogenic causes of our potential destruction, which I actually think are greater than the celestial causes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So if we get lucky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, if we get lucky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And intelligent, I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So no way will we as humans reach the heat death of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, it's conceivable that machines, which I think will be our evolutionary descendants, might reach that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Although even they will have less and less energy with which to work as time progresses because eventually even the lowest mass stars burn out, although it takes them trillions of years to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the point is that certainly on Earth there are other celestial threats, existential threats, comets, exploding stars, the sun burning out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So we will definitely need to move away from our solar system to other solar systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then the question is, can they keep on propagating to other planetary systems sufficiently long?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In our own solar system, the sun burning out is not the immediate existential threat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That'll happen in about five billion years when it becomes a red giant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Although I should hasten to add that within the next one or two billion years, the sun will have brightened enough that unless there compensatory atmospheric changes, the oceans will evaporate away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you need much less carbon dioxide for the temperatures to be maintained roughly at their present temperature and plants wouldn't like that very much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you can't lower the carbon dioxide content too much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So within one or two billion years, probably the oceans will evaporate away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But on a sooner time scale than that, I would say an asteroid collision leading to a potential mass extinction or at least an extinction of complex beings such as ourselves that require quite special conditions, unlike cockroaches and amoebas to survive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: One of these civilization changing asteroids is only one kilometer or so in diameter and bigger and a true mass extinction event is 10 kilometers or larger.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now it's true that we can find and track the orbits of asteroids that might be headed toward Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if we find them 50 or 100 years before they impact us, then clever applied physicists and engineers can figure out ways to deflect them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But at some point, some comet will come in from the deep freeze of the solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there we have very little warning months to a year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What's the deep freeze?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The deep freeze is sort of out beyond Neptune.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's this thing called the Kuiper belt and it consists of a bunch of dirty ice balls or icy dirt balls.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's the source of the comets that occasionally come close to the sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then there's an even bigger area called the scattered disk, which is sort of a big donut surrounding the solar system way out there from which other comets come.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then there's the Oort cloud, W-O-R-T after Jan Oort, a Dutch astrophysicist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it's the better part of a light year away from the sun, so a good fraction of the distance to the nearest star.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But that's like a trillion or 10 trillion comet-like objects that occasionally get disturbed by a passing star or whatever, and most of them go flying out of the solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But some go toward the sun and they come in with little warning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: By the time we can see them, they're only a year or two away from us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And moreover, not only is it hard to determine their trajectories sufficiently accurately to know whether they'll hit a tiny thing like Earth, but outgassing from the comet of gases when the ices sublimate,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: that outgassing can change the trajectory just because of conservation of momentum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's the rocket effect. Gases go out in one direction, the object moves in the other direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so since we can't predict how much outgassing there will be and in exactly what direction because these things are tumbling and rotating and stuff,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: it's hard to predict the trajectory with sufficient accuracy to know that it will hit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you certainly don't want to deflect a comet that would have missed, but you thought it was going to hit and end up having it hit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That would be like the ultimate Charlie Brown goat instead of trying to be the hero, right? He ended up being the goat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What would you do if it seemed like in a matter of months that there is some non-zero probability, maybe a high probability that there will be a collision?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: From a scientific perspective, from an engineering perspective, I imagine you would actually be in the room of people deciding what to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What philosophically to?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's a tough one, right? Because if you only have a few months, that's not much time in which to deflect it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Early detection and early action are key because when it's far away, you only have to deflect it by a tiny little angle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then by the time it reaches us, the perpendicular motion is big enough to miss Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: All you need is one radius or one diameter of the Earth, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That actually means that all you would need to do is slow it down so it arrives four minutes later or speed it up so it arrives four minutes earlier and Earth will have moved through one radius in that time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it doesn't take much, but you can imagine if a thing is about to hit you, you have to deflect it 90 degrees or more, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you don't have much time to do so and you have to slow it down or speed it up a lot if that's what you're trying to do to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Decades is sufficient time, but months is not sufficient time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: At that point, I would think the name of the game would be to try to predict where it would hit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if it's in a heavily populated region, try to start an orderly evacuation perhaps.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But that might cause just so much panic. How would you do with New York City or Los Angeles or something like that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I might have a different opinion a year ago. I'm a bit disheartened by, in the movies, there's always extreme competence from the government.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Competence, yeah. But we expect extreme incompetence, if anything, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yes, now. So I'm quite disappointed. But sort of from a medical perspective, I think you're saying there in a scientific one,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: it's almost better to get better and better, maybe telescopes and data collection to be able to predict the movement of these things or like come up with totally new technologies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You can imagine actually sending out like probes out there to be able to sort of almost have little finger sensors throughout our solar system to be able to detect stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, that's right. Yeah, monitoring the asteroid belt is very important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Ninety-nine percent of the so-called near-Earth objects ultimately come from the asteroid belt.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so there we can track the trajectories. And even if there's a close encounter between two asteroids which deflects one of them toward Earth, it's unlikely to be on a collision course with Earth in the immediate future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's more like tens of years. So that gives us time. But we would need to improve our ability to detect the objects that come in from a great distance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Unfortunately, those are much rarer. The comets come in, one percent of the collisions perhaps are with comets that come in without any warning hardly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so that might be more like a billion or two billion years before one of those hits us. So maybe we have to worry about the Sun getting brighter on that time scale.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, there's the possibility that a star will explode near us in the next couple of billion years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But over the course of the history of life on Earth, the estimates are that maybe only one of the mass extinctions was caused by a star blowing up in particular, a special kind called a gamma ray burst.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And I think it's the Ordovician-Sularian extinction, 420 or so, 440 million years ago, that is speculated to have come from one of these particular types of exploding stars called gamma ray bursts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But even there, the evidence is circumstantial. So those kinds of existential threats are reasonably rare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The greater danger, I think, is civilization changing events where it's a much smaller asteroid, which those are harder to detect, or a giant solar flare that shorts out the grid in all of North America, let's say.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, astronomers are monitoring the Sun 24-7 with various satellites, and we can tell when there's a flare or a coronal mass ejection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And we can tell that in a day or two, a giant bundle of energetic particles will arrive and twang the magnetic field of Earth and send all kinds of currents through long distance power lines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that's what shorts out the transformers. And transformers are expensive and hard to replace and hard to transport and all that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So if we can warn the power companies and they can shut down the grid before the big bundle of particle hits, then we will have mitigated much of this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, for a big enough bundle of particles, you can get short circuits even over small distance scales. So not everything will be saved, but at least the whole grid might not go out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So again, astronomers, I like to say, support your local astronomer. They may help someday save humanity by telling the power companies to shut down the grid, finding the asteroid 50 or 100 years before it hits,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: then having clever physicists and engineers deflect it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So many of these cosmic threats, cosmic existential threats, we can actually predict and do something about or observe before they hit and do something about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's terrifying to think that people would listen to this conversation. It's like when you listen to Bill Gates talk about pandemics in his Ted talk a few years ago and realizing we should have supported our local astronomer more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, I don't know whether it's more because as I said, I actually think human induced threats or things that occur naturally on Earth, either a natural pandemic or perhaps a bioengineering type pandemic,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137
