body.input: or something like a super volcano. There was one event, Toba, I think it was 70 plus thousand years ago that caused a gigantic decrease in temperatures on Earth because it sent up so much soot that it blocked the sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's the nuclear winter type disaster scenario that some people, including Carl Sagan, talked about decades ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But we can see in the history of volcanic eruptions, even more recently in the 19th century, Tambora and other ones, you look at the record and you see rather large dips in temperature associated with massive volcanic eruptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, these super volcanoes, one of which by the way exists under Yellowstone in the central US, I mean, it's not just one or two states.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's a gigantic region and there's controversy as to whether it's likely to blow anytime in the next 100,000 years or so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But that would be perhaps not a mass extinction because you really need to, or perhaps not a complete existential threat because you have to get rid of sort of the very last humans for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But at least getting rid of killing off so many humans, truly billions and billions of humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There have been ones tens of thousands of years ago, including this one, Toba I think it's called, where it's estimated that the human population was down to 10,000 or 5,000 individuals, something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If you have a 15 degree drop in temperature over quite a short time, it's not clear that even with today's advanced technology, we would be able to adequately respond, at least for the vast majority of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe some would be in these underground caves where you'd keep the president and a bunch of other important people, but the typical person is not going to be protected when all of agriculture is cut off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It could be hundreds of millions or billions of people starving to death.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Exactly. That's right. They don't all die immediately, but they use up their supplies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or again, this electrical grid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: First of toilet paper.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There you go. Dash that toilet paper. Or the electrical grid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Imagine North America without power for a year. We've become so dependent. We're no longer the cave people. They would do just fine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What do they care about the electrical grid? What do they care about agriculture? They're hunters and gatherers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But we now have become so used to our way of life that the only real survivors would be those rugged individualists who live somewhere out in the forest or in a cave somewhere, completely independent of anyone else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Recently I recommended, it's totally new to me, this kind of survivalist folks, but there's a lot of shows of those. I saw one on Netflix and I started watching them. They make a lot of sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They reveal to you how dependent we are on all aspects of this beautiful systems we humans have built and how fragile they are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Incredibly fragile.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This whole conversation is making me realize how lucky we are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We're incredibly lucky, but we've set ourselves up to be very, very fragile. We are intrinsically complex biological creatures that, except for the fact that we have brains and minds with which we can try to prevent some of these things or respond to them, we as a living organism require quite a narrow set of conditions in order to survive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We're not cockroaches. We're not going to survive a nuclear war.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We're kind of this beautiful dance between, we've been talking about astronomy, that astronomy, the stars, inspires everybody. At the same time, there's this pragmatic aspect that we're talking about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I see space exploration as the same kind of way that it's reaching out to other planets, reaching out to the stars. This really beautiful idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If you listen to somebody like Elon Musk, he talks about space exploration as very pragmatic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We have to be, he has this ridiculous way of sounding like an engineer about it, which is like, it's obvious we need to become a multi-planetary species if we were to survive long-term.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe both philosophically in terms of beauty and in terms of practical, what's your thoughts on space exploration, on the challenges of it, on how much we should be investing in it, and on a personal level, how excited you are by the possibility of going to Mars, colonizing Mars, and maybe going outside the solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, great question. There's a lot to unpack there, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Humans are by their very nature explorers, pioneers. They want to go out, climb the next mountain, see what's behind it, explore the ocean depths, explore space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This is our destiny to go out there. Of course, from a pragmatic perspective, yes, we need to plant our seeds elsewhere, really, because things could go wrong here on Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, some people say that's an excuse to not take care of our planet. Well, we say we're elsewhere, and so we don't have to take good care of our planet. No, we should take the best possible care of our planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We should be cognizant of the potential impact of what we're doing. Nevertheless, it's prudent to have us be elsewhere as well. In that regard, I actually agree with Elon. It'd be good to be on Mars. That would be yet another place for us from which to explore further.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Would that be a good next step?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, it's a good next step. I happen to disagree with him as to how quickly it will happen. I think he's very optimistic. Now, you need visionary people like Elon to get people going and to inspire them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Look at the success he's had with multiple companies. Maybe he gives this very optimistic timeline in order to be inspirational to those who are going out there. Certainly, his success with the rocket that is reusable because it landed upright and all that, that's a game changer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's sort of like every time you flew from San Francisco to Los Angeles, you discard the airplane. That's crazy. That's a game changer. Nevertheless, the time scale over which he thinks that there could be a real thriving colony on Mars, I think is far too optimistic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What's the biggest challenges to you? One is just getting rockets, not rockets, but people out there. Two is the colonization. Do you have thoughts about the challenges of this kind of prospect?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, I haven't thought about it in great detail other than recognizing that Mars is a harsh environment. You don't have much of an atmosphere there. You've got less than a percent of Earth's atmosphere. You'd need to build some sort of a dome right away, and that would take time. You need to melt the water that's in the permafrost or have canals dug from which you transport it from the polar ice caps.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I was reading recently in terms of what's the most efficient source of nutrition for humans that were to live on Mars, and people should look into this, but it turns out to be insects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Insects. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you want to build giant colonies of insects and just be eating them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Insects have a lot of protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: A lot of protein, and they're easy to grow. You can think of them as farming.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. It's not going to be as easy as growing a whole plot of potatoes like in the movie The Martian or something, right? It's not going to be that easy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there's this thin atmosphere. It's got the wrong composition. It's mostly carbon dioxide. There are these violent dust storms. The temperatures are generally cold. You'd need to do a lot of things. You need to terraform it basically in order to make it nicely livable without some dome surrounding you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if you insist on a dome, well, that's not going to house that many people, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, so let's look briefly then. We're looking for a new apartment to move into, so let's look outside the solar system. You've spoken about exoplanets as well. Do you think there's possible homes out there for us outside of our solar system?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There are lots and lots of homes, possible homes. I mean, there's a planetary system around nearly every star you see in the sky, and one in five of those is thought to have roughly Earth-like planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that's a relatively new discovery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, it's a new discovery. I mean, the Kepler satellite, which was flying around above Earth's atmosphere, was able to monitor the brightness of stars with exquisite detail, and they could detect planets crossing the line of sight between us and the star, thereby dimming its light for a short time ever so slightly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it's amazing. So there are now thousands and thousands of these exoplanet candidates, of which something like 90% are probably genuine exoplanets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you have to remember that only about 1% of stars have their planetary system oriented edge on to your line of sight, which is what you need for this transit method to work, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Some arbitrary angle won't work, and certainly perpendicular to your line of sight. That is, in the plane of the sky won't work because the planet is orbiting the star and never crossing your line of sight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the fact that they found planets orbiting about 1% of the stars that they looked at in this field of 150 plus thousand stars, they found planets around 1%.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You then multiply by the inverse of 1%, which is, right? 1% is about the fraction of the stars that have their planetary system oriented the right way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that already, back of the interval calculation, tells you that of order 50 to 100% of all stars have planets, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then they've been finding these Earth-like planets, etc., etc. So there are many potential homes. The problem is getting there, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So then a typical bright star, Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, maybe not a typical bright star, but it's 8.7 light years away, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that means the light took 8.7 years to reach us. We're seeing it as it was about nine years ago, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So then you ask, how long would a rocket take to get there at Earth's escape speed, which is 11 kilometers per second, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it turns out it's about a quarter of a million years, okay? Now that's 10,000 generations, okay? Let's say a generation of humans is 25 years, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you'd need this colony of people that is able to sustain itself, all their food, all their waste disposal, all their water, all their recycling of everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: For 10,000 generations, they have to commit themselves to living on this vehicle, right? I just don't see it happening.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What I see potentially happening, if we avoid self-destruction, intentional or unintentional, here on Earth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: is that machines will do it, robots that can essentially hibernate. They don't need to do much of anything for a long, long time as they're traveling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And moreover, if some energetic charged particles, some cosmic ray hits the circuitry, it fixes itself, right? Machines can do this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, it's a form of artificial intelligence. You just tell the thing, fix yourself basically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then when you land on the planet, start producing copies of yourself initially from materials that perhaps sent, or you just have a bunch of copies there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then they set up factories with which to do this. I mean, this is very, very futuristic, but it's much more feasible, I think, than sending flesh and blood over interstellar distances,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: a quarter of a million years to even the nearest stars. You're subject to all kinds of charged particles and radiation. You have to shield yourself really well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's, by the way, one of the problems of going to Mars is that it's not a three-day journey like going to the Moon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You're out there for the better part of a year or two, and you're exposed to lots of radiation, which typically doesn't do well with living tissue, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or if living tissue doesn't do well with the radiation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then the hope is that the robots, the AI systems might be able to carry the fire of consciousness, whatever makes us humans, like a little drop of whatever makes us humans so special, not to be too poetic about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: No, but I like being poetic about it because it's an amazing question. Is there something beyond just the bits, the ones and zeros to us? It's an interesting question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I like to think that there isn't anything and that how beautiful it is that our thoughts, our emotions, our feelings, our compassion all come from these ones and zeros, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That to me actually is a beautiful thought and the idea that machines, silicon-based life effectively could be our natural evolutionary descendants, not from a DNA perspective, but they are our creations and they then carry on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That to me is a beautiful thought in some ways, but others find it to be a horrific thought.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's exciting to you. It is exciting to me as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Because to me from a purely an engineering perspective, I believe it's impossible to create, like whatever systems we create that take over the world, it's impossible for me to imagine that those systems will not carry some aspect of what makes humans beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So like a lot of people have these kind of paperclip ideas that will build machines that are cold inside or philosophers call them zombies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That naturally the systems that will outcompete us on this earth will be cold and non-conscious, not capable of all the human emotions and empathy and compassion and love and hate, the beautiful mix of what makes us human.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But to me, intelligence requires all of that. So in order to outcompete humans, you better be good at the full picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. So artificial general intelligence in my view encompasses a lot of these attributes that you just talked about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Like curiosity, inquisitiveness, you know, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It might look very different than us humans, but it will have some of the magic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it'll also be much more able to survive the onslaught of existential threats that either we bring upon ourselves or don't anticipate here on earth, or that occasionally come from beyond.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there's nothing much we can do about a supernova explosion that just suddenly goes off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And really if we want to move to other planets outside our solar system, I think realistically that's a much better option than thinking that humans will actually make these gigantic journeys.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then I do this calculation from my class, Einstein's special theory of relativity says that you can do it in a short amount of time in your own frame of reference if you go close to the speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But then you bring in E equals MC squared and you figure out how much energy it takes to get you accelerated to close enough to the speed of light to make the time scales short in your own frame of reference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the amount of energy is just unfathomable, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We can do it at the Large Hadron Collider with protons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, we can accelerate them to 99.9999% of the speed of light, but that's just a proton.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We're gazillions of protons, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that doesn't even count the rocket that would carry us the payload.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you would need to either store the fuel in the rocket, which then requires even more mass for the rocket, or collect fuel along the way, which is difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so getting close to the speed of light, I think, is not an option either, other than for a little tiny thing like, you know, Yuri Milner and others are thinking about this, this star shot project where they'll send a little tiny camera to Alpha Centauri 4.2 light years away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They'll zip past it, take a picture of the exoplanets that we know orbit that three or more star system and say hello real quickly and then send the images back to us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that's a tiny little thing, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe you can accelerate that to their hoping 20% of the speed of light with a whole bunch of high powered lasers aimed at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's not clear that other countries will allow us to do that, by the way, but that's a very forward looking thought.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, I very much support the idea, but there's a big difference between sending a little tiny camera and sending a payload of people with equipment that could then mine the resources on the exoplanet that they reach and then go forth and multiply, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, let's talk about the big galactic things and how we might be able to leverage them to travel fast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I know this is a little bit science fiction, but you know, ideas of wormholes and ideas at the edge of black holes that reveal to us that this fabric of space time could be messed with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Perhaps is that at all an interesting thing for you? I mean, in looking out at the universe and studying it as you have, is that also a possible, like a dream for you that we might be able to find clues how we can actually use it to improve our transportation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's an interesting thought. I'm certainly excited by the potential physics that suggests this kind of faster than light travel effectively or cutting the distance to make it very, very short through a wormhole or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Possible? No.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, you know, call me not very imaginative, but based on today's knowledge of physics, which I realize, you know, people have gone down that rabbit hole and, you know, a century ago, Lord Kelvin, one of the greatest physicists of all time said that all of fundamental physics is done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The rest is just engineering and guess what? Then came special relativity, quantum physics, general relativity, how wrong he was. So let me not be another Lord Kelvin.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: On the other hand, I think we know a lot more now about what we know and what we don't know and what the physical limitations are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And to me, most of these schemes, if not all of them, seem very far-fetched, if not impossible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So travel through wormholes, for example. You know, it appears that for a non-rotating black hole, that's just a complete no-go because the singularity is a point-like singularity and you have to reach it to traverse the wormhole and you get squished by the singularity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Okay. Now for a rotating black hole, it turns out there is a way to pass through the event horizon, the boundary of the black hole, and avoid the singularity and go out the other side or even traverse the donut hole-like singularity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In the case of a rotating black hole, it's a ring singularity. So there's actually two theoretical ways you could get through a rotating black hole or a charged black hole,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: not that we expect charged black holes to exist in nature because they would quickly bring in the opposite charge so as to neutralize themselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But rotating black holes, definitely a reality. We now have good evidence for them. Do they have traversable wormholes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Probably not because it's still the case that when you go in, you go in with so much energy that it either squeezes the wormhole shut or you encounter a whole bunch of incoming and outgoing energy that vaporizes you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's called the mass inflation instability and it just sort of vaporizes you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Nevertheless, you could imagine, well, you're in some vapor form, but if you make it through, maybe you could reform or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it's still information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, it's still information. It's scrambled information, but there's a way maybe of bringing it back, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But then the thing that really bothers me is that as soon as you have this possibility of traversal of a wormhole, you have to come to grips with a fundamental problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that is that you could come back to your universe at a time prior to your leaving and you could essentially prevent your grandparents from ever meeting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This is called the grandfather paradox, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if they never met and if your parents were never born and if you were never born, how would you have made the journey to prevent the history from allowing you to exist, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's a violation of causality, of cause and effect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, physicists such as myself take causality violation very, very seriously.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We've never seen it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You took a stand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, I mean, you know, it's one of these right back to the future type movies, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you have to work things out in such a way that you don't mess things up, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Some people say that, well, you come back to the universe, but you come back in such a way that you cannot affect your journey.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But then, I mean, that seems kind of contrived to me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or some say that you end up in a different universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And this also goes into the many different types of the multiverse hypothesis and the many worlds interpretation and all that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But again, then it's not the universe from which you left, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you don't come back to the universe from which you left.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so you're not really going back in time to the same universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you're not even going forward in time necessarily then to the same universe, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You're ending up in some other universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So what have you achieved, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You traveled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You traveled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You ended up in a different place than you started in more ways than one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, and then there's this idea, the Alcubierre drive, where you warp space-time in front of you so as to greatly reduce the distance and you can expand the space-time behind you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you're sort of riding a wave through space-time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the problem I see with that, beyond the practical difficulties and the energy requirements, and by the way, how do you get out of this bubble through which you're riding this wave of space-time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And Miguel Alcubierre acknowledged all these things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: He said this is purely theoretical, fanciful and all that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But a fundamental problem I see is that you'd have to get to those places in front of you so as to change the shape of space-time so as to make the journey quickly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But to get there, you got there in the normal way at a speed considerably less than that of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So in a sense, you haven't saved any time, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You might as well have just taken that journey and gotten to where you were going.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, there's a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What have you done?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's not like you snap your fingers and say, okay, let that space there be compressed and then I'll make it over to Alpha Centauri in the next month.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You can't snap your fingers and do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, but yeah, we're sort of assuming that we can fix all the biological stuff that requires for humans to persist through that whole process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Because ultimately it might boil down to just extending the life of the human in some form, whether it's through the robot, through the digital form or actually just figuring out genetically how to live forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That journey that you mentioned, the long journey, might be different if somehow our understanding of genetics, our understanding of our own biology, all that kind of stuff would...

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's another trajectory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. If you could put us into some sort of suspended animation, hibernation or something and greatly increase the lifetime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: These 10,000 generations I talked about, what do they care? It's just one generation and they're asleep.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's a long nap.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Then you can do it. It's still not easy because you've got some big old huge colony and that just through E equals MC squared.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's a lot of mass. That's a lot of stuff to accelerate. The Newtonian kinetic energy is gigantic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You're still not home free, but at least you're not trying to do it in a short amount of clock time, which if you look at E equals MC squared requires truly unfathomable amounts of energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Because the energy is your rest mass, M not C squared divided by the square root of one minus V squared over C squared.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If your listeners want to just sort of stick into their pocket calculator as V over C approaches one, that one over the square root of one minus V squared over C squared approaches infinity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If you wanted to do it in zero time, you'd need an infinite amount of energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's basically why you can't reach, let alone exceed the speed of light for a particle moving through a pre-existing space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's that it takes an infinite amount of energy to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that's talking about us going somewhere. What about one of the things that inspires a lot of folks, including myself, is the possibility that there's other that this this conversation is happening and another planet in different forms with intelligent life forms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, first we could start as a cosmologist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What's your intuition about whether there is or isn't intelligent life out there outside of our own?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, I would say I'm one of the pessimists in that I don't necessarily think that we're the only ones in the observable universe, which goes out roughly 14 billion years in light travel time and more like 46 billion years when you take into account the expansion of space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the diameter of our observable universe is something like 90, 92 billion light years. That encompasses 100 billion to a trillion galaxies with 100 billion stars each.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So now you're talking about something like 10 to the 22nd, 10 to the 23rd power stars and roughly an equal number of Earth-like planets and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there may well be other intelligent life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But your sense is our galaxy is not teeming with life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, our galaxy, our Milky Way galaxy with several hundred billion stars and potentially habitable planets is not teeming with intelligent life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Intelligent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, well, I'll get to the primitive life, the bacteria in a moment, but we may well be the only ones in our Milky Way galaxy, at most a handful I'd say, but I'd probably side with the school of thought that suggests we're the only ones in our own galaxy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Just because I don't see human intelligence as being a natural evolutionary path for life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, there's a number of arguments. First of all, there's been more than 10 billion species of life on Earth in its history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Nothing has approached our level of intelligence and mechanical ability and curiosity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Whales and dolphins appear to be reasonably intelligent, but there's no evidence that they can think abstract thoughts that they're curious about the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They certainly can't build machines with which to study the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that's one argument.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Secondly, we came about as early hominids only four or five million years ago and as homo sapiens only about a quarter of a million years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So for the vast majority of the history of life on Earth, an intelligent alien zipping by Earth would have said there's nothing particularly intelligent or mechanically able on Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Thirdly, it's not clear that our intelligence is a long-term evolutionary advantage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now it's clear that in the last 100 years, 200 years, we've improved the lives of millions, hundreds of millions of people, but at the risk of potentially destroying ourselves either intentionally or unintentionally or through neglect as we discussed before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's a really interesting point, which is it's possible that there a huge amount of intelligent civilizations have been born even through our galaxy, but they live very briefly and they flash bulbs and the flight flight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That brings me to the fourth issue.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that is the Fermi paradox.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If they're common, where the hell are they?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Notwithstanding the various UFO reports in Roswell and all that, they just don't meet the bar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They don't clear the bar of scientific evidence in my opinion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there's no clear evidence that they've ever visited us on Earth here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And SETI has been now the search for extraterrestrial intelligence has been scanning the skies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And true, we've only looked a couple of hundred light years out and that's a tiny fraction of the whole galaxy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: A tiny fraction of these hundred billion plus stars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Nevertheless, if the galaxy were teeming with life, especially intelligent life, you'd expect some of it to have been far more advanced than ours.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's nothing special about when the Industrial Revolution started on Earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The chemical evolution of our galaxy was such that billions of years ago, nuclear processing and stars had built up clouds of gas after their explosion that were rich enough and heavy elements to have formed Earth-like planets, even billions of years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there could be civilizations that are billions of years ahead of ours.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if you look at the exponential growth of technology among Homo sapiens in the last couple of hundred years and you just project that forward, there's no telling what they could have achieved even in 1000 or 10,000 years, let alone a million or 10 million or a billion years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if they reach this capability of interstellar travel and colonization, then you can show that within 10 million years or certainly 100 million years, you can populate the whole galaxy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So then you don't have to have tried to detect them beyond 100 or 1000 light years. They would already be here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Do you think as a thought experiment, do you think it's possible that they are already here, but we humans are so human-centric that our conception of what intelligent life looks like, we don't want to acknowledge it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Like what if trees? Right. Right. Right. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Okay. I guess in the form of a question, do you think we'll actually detect intelligent life if it came to visit us?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. I mean, it's like, you know, you're an ant crawling around on a sidewalk somewhere and do you notice the humans wandering around? Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the Empire State building and, you know, rocket ships flying to the moon and all that kind of stuff. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's conceivable that we haven't detected it and that we're so primitive compared to them that we're just not able to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Like if you look at dark energy, maybe we call it as a field.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's just that my own feeling is that in science now through observations and experiments, we've measured so many things and basically we understand a lot of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Fabric of reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. The fabric of reality we understand quite well and there are a few little things like dark matter and dark energy that may be some sign of some super intelligence, but I doubt it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Okay. You know, why would some super intelligence be holding clusters of galaxies together?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Why would they be responsible for accelerating the expansion of the universe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the point is, is that through science and applied science and engineering, we understand so much now that I'm not saying we know everything, but we know a hell of a lot. Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so it's not like there are lots of mysteries flying around there that are completely outside our level of exploration or understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. From a, I would say from, from the mystery perspective, it seems like the mystery of our own cognition and consciousness is much grander than like the degrees of freedom of possible explanations of what the heck is going on is much greater there than in the, in the physics of the observable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: How the brain works. How did life arise? Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's big, big questions, but they, to me, don't indicate the existence of, of, of, of an alien or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, unless we are the aliens, you know, we could have been contamination from some rocket ship that, that hit here a long, long time ago and all evidence of it has been destroyed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But again, that alien would have started out somewhere. They're not, they're not here watching us right now, right? They're not among us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so though there are expl, potential explanations for the Fermi paradox, and one of them that I kind of like is that the truly intelligent creatures are those that decided not to colonize the whole galaxy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Cause they'd quickly run out of room there because it's exponential, right? You send a probe to a planet. It makes two copies. They go out. They make two copies each and it's an exponential, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They quickly colonize the whole galaxy, but then the distance to the next galaxy, the next big one, like Andromeda, that's two and a half million light years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's a much grander scale now, right? And so it, it also could be that the reason they survived this long is that they got over this tendency that may well exist among sufficiently intelligent creatures, this tendency for aggression and self destruction, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If they bypass that, and that may be one of the great filters, if there are more than one, right? Then they may not be a type of creature that feels the need to go and say, Oh, there's a nice looking planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there's a bunch of ants on it. Let's go squish them and colonize it. No, it could even be the kind of Star Trek like prime directive where you go and explore worlds, but you don't interfere in any way. Right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And also we call it exploration is beautiful and everything, but there is underlying this desire to explore is a desire to conquer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, if we're just being really honest about-

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right now for us it is, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you're saying it's possible to separate, but I would venture to say that you wouldn't, that those are coupled. So I could, I could imagine a civilization that lives on for billions of years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That just stays on us, like figures out the minimal effort way of just peacefully existing. It's like a monastery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. And it limits itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, it's planted its seeds in a number of places, so it's not vulnerable to a single point failure, right? Supernova going off near one of these stars or something, or an asteroid or a comet coming in from the Oort cloud equivalent of that planetary system and without warning, you know, thrashing them to bits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So they've got their seeds in a bunch of places, but they chose not to colonize the galaxy. And they also choose not to interfere with this incredibly prevalent primitive organism, homo sapiens. Right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or they, this is like a, they enjoy, this is like a TV show for them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, it could be like a TV show, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So they just tuned in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. So those are possible explanations. Yet I think that to me, the most likely explanation for the Fermi paradox is that they really are very, very rare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you know, Carl Sagan estimated a hundred thousand of them. If there's that many, some of them would have been way ahead of us. And, and I think we would have seen them by now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If there are a handful, maybe they're there, but at that point you're right on this dividing line between being a pessimist and an optimist. And what are the odds for that? Right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If you look at all the things that had to go right for us. And then, you know, getting back to something you said earlier, let's discuss, you know, primitive life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That could be the thing that's difficult to achieve. Just getting the random molecules together to a point where they start self replicating and evolving and becoming better and all that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That, that's an inordinately difficult thing. I think, though I'm not, you know, some molecular cell biologist, but just it's, it's, it's the usual argument.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, you're wandering around in the Sahara desert and you stumble across a watch is your, is your initial response. Oh, you know, a bunch of sand grains just came together randomly and formed this watch.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: No, you, you think that something formed it or it came from some simpler structure that then became, you know, more complex. All right. It didn't just form.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, even the simplest life is, is a very, very complex structure. Even the, even the simplest prokaryotic cells, not to mention eukaryotic cells, although that transition may have been the so-called great filter as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe the cells without a nucleus are relatively easy to form. And then the big next step is where you have a nucleus, which then provides a lot of energy, which allows the cell to become much, much more complex and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Interestingly, going from eukaryotic cells, single cells to multicellular organisms does not appear to be at least on earth. One of these great filters, because there's evidence that it happened dozens of times independently on earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So by, by a really great filter, something that happens very, very rarely, I mean that we had to get through an obstacle that is just incredibly rare to get through.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And one of the really exciting scientific things is that that particular point is something that we might be able to discover even in our lifetimes that find life elsewhere, like Europa or be able to see.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That would be bad news. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Cause if we find lots of pretty advanced life, that would suggest, and especially if we found some, you know, defunct, you know, fossilized civilization or something somewhere else, that would be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh, bacteria you mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What's that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Defunct civilization of like primitive life forms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I'm sorry. I switched gears there. If we, if we found some intelligent or rather, you know, even trilobites, right. And stuff, you know, elsewhere, that would be bad news for us because that would mean that the great filter is ahead of us. You know, right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Because it would mean that lots of, lots of things have gotten roughly to our level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, but given the Fermi paradox, if you accept that the Fermi paradox means that there's no one else out there, you don't necessarily have to accept that. But if you accept that it means that no one else is out there and yet there are lots of things we found that are at or roughly at our level, that means that the great filter is ahead of us and that bodes poorly for our longterm future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, yeah, it's funny. You said, uh, you started by saying you're a little bit on the pessimistic side, but it's funny because we're doing this kind of dance between pessimism and optimism because I'm not sure if us being alone in the observable universe as intelligent beings is pessimistic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, it's good news in a sense for us because it means that we made it through.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh, right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: See, if we're the only ones and there are such great filters, maybe more than one formation of life might be one of them. Formation of eukaryotic that is with the nucleus cells be another development of human-like intelligence might be another, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There might be several such filters and we were the lucky ones. And, you know, then people say, well, then that means you're putting yourself into a special perspective.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And every time we've done that, we've been wrong. And yeah, yeah, I know all those arguments, but it still could be the case that there's one of us, at least per galaxy or pretend or a hundred or a thousand galaxies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And we're sitting here having this conversation because we exist. And so there's a, there's an observational selection effect there, right? Just because we're special doesn't mean that we shouldn't have these conversations about whether or not we're special, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. So that's, that's exciting. That's optimistic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that's the, that's the optimistic part that if we don't find other intelligent life there, it might mean that we're the ones that made it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And in general, outside the great filter and so on, you know, it's not obvious that the Stephen Hawking thing, which is, it's not obvious that life out there is going to be kind to us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So, you know, I knew Hawking and I greatly respect his scientific work. And in particular, the early work on the unification of general theory of relativity and quantum physics to two great pillars in modern physics, you know, Hawking radiation and all that fantastic work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, if you were alive, he should have been a recipient of this year's physics Nobel prize, which was for the discovery of black holes and also by Roger Penrose for the theoretical work showing that given a star that's massive enough, you basically can't avoid having a black hole.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Anyway, Hawking, fantastic. I tip my hat to him. May he rest in peace.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That would have been a heck of a Nobel prize. Black holes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137
