body.input: But going back to what he said that we shouldn't be broadcasting our presence to others, there I actually disagree with him respectfully because first of all, we've been unintentionally broadcasting our presence for a hundred years since the development of radio and TV.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Secondly, any alien that has the capability of coming here and squashing us, either already knows about us and, you know, doesn't care because we're just like little ants.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And when there are ants in your kitchen, you tend to squash them. But if there are ants on the sidewalk and you're walking by, do you feel some great conviction that you have to squash any of them?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: No, you generally don't, right? We're irrelevant to them. All they need to do is keep an eye on us to see whether we're approaching the kind of technological capability and know about them and have intentions of attacking them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then they can squash us, right? They could have done it long ago. They'll do it if they want to. Whether we advertise our presence or not is irrelevant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So I really think that that's not a huge existential threat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So this is a good place to bring up a difficult topic. You mentioned they would be paying attention to us to see if we come up with any crazy technology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's folks who have reported UFO sightings. There's actually, I've recently found out there's websites that track this, the data of these reportings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there's millions of them in the past several decades, seven decades and so on, that they've been recorded.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the UFOlogist community, as they refer to themselves, one of the ideas that I find compelling from an alien perspective, that they kind of started showing up ever since we figured out how to build nuclear weapons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What a coincidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So I mean, if I was an alien, I would start showing up then as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, why not just observe us from afar?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I know, right. I would figure out. But that's why I'm always keeping a distance and staying blurry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. Very pixelated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Very pixelated. You know, there is something in the human condition that a cognition that wants to see, wants to believe beautiful things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And some are terrifying. Some are exciting. Goats. Bigfoot is a big fascination for folks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And UFO sightings, I think falls into that. There's people that look at lights in the night sky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, it's kind of a downer to think in a skeptical sense, to think that's just the light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You want to feel like there's something magical there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, I felt that first when my dad, my dad's a physicist, when he first told me about ball lightning, when I was like a little kid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Very weird.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Very like weird physical phenomena. And he said his intuition was, tell me this as a little kid, like I really like math.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: His intuition was whoever figures out ball lightning will get a Nobel Prize.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I think that was a side comment he gave me. I decided there when I was like five years old or whatever, I'm going to win a Nobel Prize for figuring out ball lightning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That was like one of the first sort of sparks of the scientific mindset. Those mysteries, they capture your imagination.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I think when I speak to people that report UFOs, that's that fire. That's what I see. That excitement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I understand that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But what do we do with that? Because there's hundreds of thousands, if not millions, and then the scientific community, you're like the perfect person.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You have an awesome Einstein shirt. What do we do with those reports?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Most of the scientific community kind of rolls their eyes and dismisses it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Is it possible that a tiny percent of those folks saw something that's worth deeply investigating?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure. We should investigate it. It's just one of these things where they've not brought us a hunk of kryptonite or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They haven't brought us actual, tangible physical evidence with which experiments can be done in laboratories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's anecdotal evidence. The photographs are, in some cases, in most cases, I would say quite ambiguous.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't know what to think about. So David Fravor is the first person. He's a Navy pilot commander.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's a bunch of them, but he's one of the most legit pilots and people I've ever met.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The fact that he saw something weird, he doesn't know what the heck it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: He saw something weird. I don't know what to do with that. On the psychological side, I'm pretty confident he saw what he says he saw, which he's saying is something weird.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: One of the interesting psychological things that worries me is that everybody in the Navy, everybody in the US government, everybody in the scientific community just kind of pretended that nothing happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That kind of instinct, that's what makes me believe if aliens show up, we would all just ignore their presence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's what bothered me, that you don't investigate it more carefully and use this opportunity to inspire the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In terms of kryptonite, I think the conspiracy theory folks say that whenever there is some good hard evidence that scientists would be excited about, there's this kind of conspiracy that I don't like because it's ultimately negative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That the US government will somehow hide the good evidence to protect it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Of course, there's some legitimacy to it because you want to protect military secrets, all that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't know what to do with this beautiful mess because I think millions of people are inspired by UFOs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It feels like an opportunity to inspire people about science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I would say, as Carl Sagan used to say, extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I've quoted him a number of times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We would welcome such evidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: On the other hand, a lot of the things that are seen or perhaps even hidden from us, you could imagine for military purposes, surveillance purposes, the US government doesn't want us to know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or maybe some of these pilots saw Soviet or Israeli or whatever satellites.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Some of the crashes that have occurred were later found to be weather balloons or whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: When there are more conventional explanations, science tends to stay away from the sensational ones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It may be that someone else's calling in life is to investigate these phenomena.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I welcome that as a scientist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't categorically actually deny the possibility that ships of some sort could have visited us because, as I said earlier, at slow speeds, there's no problem in reaching other stars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In fact, our Voyager and Pioneer spacecraft in a few million years are going to be in the vicinity of different stars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We can even calculate which ones they're going to be in the vicinity of.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's nothing that breaks any laws of physics if you do it slowly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But that's different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Just having Voyager or Pioneer fly by some star, that's different from having active aliens altering the trajectory of their vehicle in real time, spying on us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: and then either zipping back to their home planet or sending signals that tell them about us because they are likely many light years away and they're not going to have broken that barrier as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Go ahead, study them. Great. For some young kid who wants to do it, it might be their calling. That's how they might find meaning in their lives, is to be the scientist who really explores these things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I chose not to because at a very young age I found the evidence to the degree that I investigated it to be really quite unconvincing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I had other things that I wanted to do. But I don't categorically deny the possibility and I think it should be investigated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This is one of those phenomena that 99.9% of people are almost definitely there's conventional explanations and then there's mysterious things that probably have explanations that are a little bit more complicated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But there's not enough to work with. I tend to believe that if aliens showed up, there will be plenty of evidence for scientists to study.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Exactly, as you said, avoid your type of spacecraft. I could see some kind of a dumb thing, almost like a sensor, like statistically speaking, flying by, maybe lands, maybe there's some kind of robot type of thingies that just move around and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Like in ways that we don't understand. But I feel like there will be plenty of hard to dismiss evidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And I also, especially this year, believe that the US government is not sufficiently competent, given the huge amount of evidence that will be revealed from this kind of thing, to conceal all of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: At least in modern times, you can say maybe decades ago, but in modern times. But the people I speak to and the reason I bring it up is because so many people write to me, they're inspired by it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: By the way, I wanted to comment on something you said earlier. I had said that I'm sort of a pessimist in that I think there are very few other intelligent, mechanically able creatures out there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But then I said, yes, in a sense, I'm an optimist, as you pointed out, because it means that we made it through the great filter. I meant originally that I'm a pessimist in that I'm pessimistic about the possibility that there are many, many of us out there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Mathematically speaking, in the Drake equation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Exactly. But it may mean a good thing for our ultimate survival. So I'm glad you caught me on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, I definitely agree with you. It is ultimately an optimistic statement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But anyway, I think UFO research is interesting. And I guess one of the reasons I've not been terribly convinced is that I think there are some scientists who are investigating this and they've not found any clear evidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, I must admit I have not looked through the literature to convince myself that there are many scientists doing systematic studies of these various reports. So I can't say for sure that there's a critical mass of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it's just that you never get these reports from hardcore scientists. That's the other thing. And astronomers, what do we do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We spend our time studying the heavens and you'd think we'd be the ones that are most likely, aside from pilots perhaps, at seeing weird things in the sky. And we just never do of the unexplained UFO type nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, I try to keep an open mind. But for people who listen, it's actually really difficult for scientists. Like this year, I've probably gotten over a thousand emails on the topic of AGI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's very difficult to... People write to me, it's like, how can you ignore this in AGI side, like this model? This is obviously the model that's going to achieve general intelligence. How can you ignore it? I'm giving you the answer. Here's my document.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there's always just these large write-ups. The problem is, it's very difficult to weed through a bunch of BS. It's very possible that you actually saw the UFO, but you have to acknowledge, by UFO I mean an extraterrestrial life, you have to acknowledge the hundreds of thousands of people who are a little bit, if not a lot, full of BS.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And from a scientist perspective, it's really hard work. When there's amazing stuff out there, it's like, why investigate Bigfoot when evolution and all of its richness is beautiful? Who cares about a monkey that walks on two feet or eight or whatever?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sometimes it's like there's a zillion decoys at observatories. True fact, we get lots and lots of phone calls when Venus, the evening star, but just really a bright planet happens to be close to the crescent moon because it's such a striking pair. This happens once in a while.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You get these phone calls, oh, there's a UFO next to the moon. And no, it's Venus. And I'm not saying the best UFO reports are of that nature. No, there are some much more convincing cases and I've seen some of the footage and blah, blah, blah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it's just there's so many decoys, right? So much noise that you have to filter out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there's only so many scientists, so it's hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's only so much time as well and you have to choose what problems you work on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This might be a fun question to ask to kind of explore the idea of the expanding universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the radius of the observable universe is 45.7 billion light years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the age of the universe is 13.7 billion years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's less than the radius of the universe. How's that possible?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that's a great question. So I meant to bring a little prop I have with ping pong balls on a rubber hose, a rubber band.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I use it in many of the lectures that one can find of me online. But you have in an expanding universe, the space itself between galaxies or more correctly, clusters of galaxies expanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So imagine light going from one cluster to another. It traverses some distance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then while it's traversing the rest, that part that it already traveled through continues to expand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, 13.7 billion years might have gone by since the light that we are seeing from the early stages, the so-called cosmic microwave background radiation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: which is the afterglow of the Big Bang or the echo of the Big Bang. Yeah, 13.7 billion years have gone by.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's how long it's taken that light to reach us. But while it's been traveling that distance, the parts that it already traveled continue to expand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it's like you're walking on at an airport on one of these walkways and you're walking along because you're trying to get to your terminal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the walkway is continuing as well. You end up traveling a greater distance or the same distance faster is another way of putting it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's why you get on one of these traveling walkways. So you get roughly a factor of pi, but it's more like 3.2, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But when you work it all out, you multiply the number of years the universe has been in existence by three and a quarter or so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that's how you get this 46 billion light year radius.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But how is that? Let me ask some nice dumb questions. How is that not traveling faster than the speed of light?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, it's not traveling faster than the speed of light because locally at any point if you were to measure the light, the photon zipping past, it would not be exceeding the speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The speed of light is a locally measured quantity. After light has traversed some distance, if the rubber band keeps on stretching, then yes, it looks like the light traveled a greater distance than it would have had the space not been expanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But locally it never was exceeding the speed of light. It's just that the distance through which it already traveled then went off and expanded on its own some more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if you give the light credit, so to speak, for having traversed that distance, well then it looks like it's going faster than the speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But that's not how speed works.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right, that's not how speed works. And in relativity also the other thing that is interesting is that if you take two ping pong balls that are sufficiently far apart, especially in an accelerating universe, you can easily have them moving apart from one another faster than the speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So, you know, take two ping pong balls that were originally 400,000 kilometers from each other and let every centimeter in your rubber band expand to two in one second.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Then suddenly this 400,000 kilometer distance is 800,000 kilometers. It went out by 400,000 kilometers in one second. That exceeds the 300,000 kilometer per second speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But that light limit, that particle limit in special relativity applies to objects moving through a pre-existing space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's nothing in either special or general relativity that prevents space itself from expanding faster than the speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's no problem. Einstein wouldn't have had a problem with a universe as observed now by cosmologists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, I'm not sure I'm yet ready to deal emotionally with expanding space. That to me is one of the most awe-inspiring things, you know, starting from the Big Bang.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's definitely abstract.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Space itself is expanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Could you, can we talk about the Big Bang a little bit?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure. Yeah, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So like the entirety of it, the universe was very small.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. But it was not a point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It was not a point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Because if we live in what's called a closed universe now, a sphere or the three dimensional version of that would be a hypersphere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Then regardless of how far back in time you go, it was always that topological shape. You can't turn a point suddenly into a shell. Okay. It always had to be a shell.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So when people say, well, the universe started out as a point, that's being kind of flippant, kind of glib. It didn't really. It just started out at a very high density.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And we don't know actually whether it was finite or infinite. I think personally that it was finite at the time, but it expanded very, very quickly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Indeed, if it exponentiated and continued in some places to exponentiate, then it could in fact be infinite right now. And most cosmologists think that it is infinite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Wait, wait, wait. Sorry. Infinite in which dimension? Mass, size?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Infinite in space. Infinite in space. And by that I mean that if you were trying to measure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's no boundary. Use light to measure its size. You'd never be able to measure its size because it would always be bigger than the distance light can travel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's what you get in a universe that's accelerating in its expansion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Okay. But if a thing was a hypersphere, it's very small, not a point. Yeah. How can that thing be infinite?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, it expands exponentially. That's what the inflation theory is all about. Indeed, at your home institution, Alan Guth is one of the originators of the whole inflationary universe idea,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: along with Andrei Linde at Stanford University here in the Bay Area and others, Alexei Starobinsky and others had similar sorts of ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But in an exponentially expanding universe, if you actually try to make this measurement, you send light out to try to see it curve back around and hit you in the back of the head.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If it's an exponentially expanding universe, the amount of space remaining to be traversed is always a bigger and bigger quantity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you'll never get there from here. You'll never reach the back of your head.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So observationally or operationally, it can be thought of as being infinite. That's one of the best definitions of infinity, by the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's one of the best sort of physical manifestations of infinity. Yeah, yeah. Because you have to ask how would you actually measure it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, I sometimes say to my cosmology theoretical friends, well, if I took, if I were God and I were outside this whole thing and I took a God-like slice in time,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: wouldn't it be finite no matter how big it is? And they object and they say, Alex, you can't be outside and take a God-like slice of time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Because there's nothing outside.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, I'm not, you know, or also, you know, what slice of time you're taking depends on your motion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that's true even in special relativity that slices of time get tilted in a sense if you're moving quickly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The axes, X and T actually become tilted, not perpendicular to one another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And, you know, you can look at Brian Greene's books and lectures and other things where he imagines taking a loaf of bread and slicing it in units of time as you progress forward.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But then if you're zipping along relative to that loaf of bread, the slices of time actually become tilted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so it's not even clear what slices of time mean. But I'm an observational astronomer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I know which end of the telescope to look through. And the way I understand the infinity is, as I just told you, that operationally or observationally,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: there'd be no way of seeing that it's a finite universe, of measuring a finite universe. And so in that sense, it's infinite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Even if it started out as a finite little dot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, not a dot, I'm sorry, a finite little hypersphere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it didn't really start out there because what happened before that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, we don't know. So this is where it gets into a lot of speculation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Let's go there. Okay, sure. So, you know, nobody can prove me wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. What happened before t equals zero and whether there are other universes out there. I like to say that these are sort of on the boundaries of science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They're not just ideas that we wake up at three in the morning to go to the bathroom and say, oh, well, let's think about what happened before the Big Bang or let there be a multiplicity of universes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In other words, we have real testable physics that we can use to draw certain conclusions that are plausibility arguments based on what we know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, admittedly, there are not really direct tests of these hypotheses. That's why I call them hypotheses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They're not really elevated to a theory because a theory in science is really something that has a lot of experimental or observational support behind it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So they're hypotheses, but they're not unreasonable hypotheses based on what we know about general relativity and quantum physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And they may have indirect tests in that if you adopt this hypothesis, then there might be a bunch of things you expect of the universe and lo and behold, that's what we measure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But we're not actually measuring anything at t less than zero or we're not actually measuring the presence of another universe in this multiverse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And yet there are these indirect ideas that stem forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it's hard to prove uniqueness and it's hard to completely convince oneself that a certain hypothesis must be true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the more and more tests you have that it satisfies, let's say there are 50 predictions it makes and 49 of them are things that you can measure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then the 50th one is the one where you want to measure the actual existence of that other universe or what happened before t equals zero.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you can't do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But you've satisfied 49 of the other testable predictions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so that's science, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now, a conventional condensed matter physicist or someone who deals with real data in the laboratory might say, oh, you cosmologists, that's not really science because it's not directly testable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But I would say it's sort of testable, but it's not completely testable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so it's at the boundary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it's not like we're coming up with these crazy ideas among them quantum fluctuations out of nothing and then inflating into a universe with the same quantum

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: fluctuations out of nothing and then inflating into a universe with you might say, well, you created a giant amount of energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But in fact, this quantum fluctuation out of nothing, you know, in a quantum way violates the conservation of energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, you know, who cares? That was a classical law anyway.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then an inflating universe maintains whatever energy it had, be it zero or some infinitesimal amount.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In a sense, the stuff of the universe has a positive energy, but there's a negative gravitational energy associated with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's like I drop an apple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I got kinetic energy, energy of motion out of that, but I did work on it to bring it to that height.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So by going down and gaining energy of motion, positive one, two, three, four, five units of kinetic energy, it's also gaining or losing, depending on how you want to think of it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: negative one, two, three, four, five units of potential energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the total energy remains the same and inflating universe can do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Or other physicists say that energy isn't conserved in general relativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's another way out of creating a universe out of nothing, you know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the point is that this is all based on reasonably well tested physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And although these extrapolations seem kind of outrageous at first, they're not completely outrageous.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They're within the realm of what we call science already.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And maybe some young whippersnapper will be able to figure out a way to directly test what happened before T equals zero or to test for the presence of these other universes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But right now we don't have a way of doing that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So speaking of young whippersnappers, Roger Penrose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So he kind of has a, you know, idea that we, there may be some information that travels from whatever the heck happened before the big bang.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Is that kind of doubt it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Do you think it's possible to detect something like actually experimentally be able to detect some, I don't know what it is, radiation, some, some sort of cosmic microwave background radiation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There may be ways of doing that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But is it, is it philosophically or practically possible to detect signs that this was before the big bang or is it, or is it what you said, which is like everything we observe will, as we currently understand, will have to be a creation of this particular observable universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. I mean, you know, a few, it's very difficult to answer right now because we don't have a single verified, fully self-consistent, experimentally tested quantum theory of gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And of course the beginning of the universe is a large amount of stuff in a very small space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you need both quantum mechanics and general relativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Same thing if our universe recollapses and then bounces back to another big bang.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, there's also ideas there that some of the information leaks through or survives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't know that we can answer that question right now because we don't have a quantum theory of gravity that most physicists believe in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And belief is perhaps the wrong word that most physicists trust because the experimental evidence favors it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, there are various forms of string theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's quantum loop gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There are various ideas, but which if any will be the one that survives the test of time and more importantly within that, the test of experiment and observation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So my own feeling is probably these things don't survive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't think we've seen any evidence in the cosmic microwave background radiation of information leaking through.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Similarly, the one way or one of the few ways in which we might test for the presence of other universes is if they were to collide with ours.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That would leave a pattern, a temperature signature in the cosmic microwave background radiation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Some astrophysicists claim to have found it, but in my opinion, it's not statistically significant to the level that would be necessary to have such an amazing claim.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. You know, it's just a 5% chance that the microwave background had that distribution just by chance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: 5% isn't very long odds if you're claiming that instead that you're finding evidence from another universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, it's like if the Large Hadron Collider people had claimed after gathering enough data to show the Higgs particle,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: when there was a 5% chance it could be just a statistical fluctuation in their data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: No, they required five sigma, five standard deviations, which is roughly one chance in 2 million that this is a statistical fluctuation of no physical greater significance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It all boils down to that. And the greater your claim, the greater is the evidence that is needed and the more evidence you need from independent ways of measuring or of coming to that deduction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: A good example was the accelerating universe. When we found evidence for it in 1998 with supernovae with exploding stars,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: it was great that there were two teams that lent some credibility to the discovery. But it was not until other astrophysicists used not only that technique,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: but more importantly, other independent techniques that had their own potential sources of systematic error or whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But they all came to the same conclusion and that started giving a much more complete picture of what was going on and a picture in which most astrophysicists quickly gained confidence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's why that idea caught on so quickly is that there were other physicists and astronomers doing observations completely independent of supernovae that seemed to indicate the same thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, that period of your life that work with an incredible team of people that won the Nobel Prize is just fascinating work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh gosh, you know, never in my wildest dreams as a kid did I think that I would be involved, much less so heavily involved, in a discovery that's so revolutionary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, you know, as a kid, as a scientist, if you're realistic, once you learn a little bit more about how science is done and you're not going to win a Nobel Prize and be the next Newton or Einstein or whatever,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: you just hope that you'll contribute something to humankind's understanding of how nature works and you'll be satisfied with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But here I was in the right place at the right time, a lot of luck, a lot of hard work. And there it was.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We discovered something that was really amazing and that was the greatest thrill, right? I couldn't have asked for anything more than being involved in that discovery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the couple of teams, the Supernova Cosmology Project and the Hi-Z Supernova Search team, what was the Nobel Prize given for?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It was given for the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Not for the elucidation of what dark energy is or what causes that expansion, that acceleration, be it universes on the outside or whatever. It was only for the observational fact.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So first of all, what is the accelerating universe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So the accelerating universe is simply that if we look at the galaxies moving away from us right now, we would expect them to be moving away more slowly than they were billions of years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that's because galaxies have visible matter, which is gravitationally attractive, and dark matter of an unknown sort that holds galaxies together and holds clusters of galaxies together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And of course, they then pull on one another and they would tend to retard the expansion of the universe, just as when I toss an apple up, even ignoring air resistance, the mutual gravitational attraction between Earth and the apple slows the apple down.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if that attraction is great enough, then the apple will someday stop and even come back. The Big Crunch, you could call it, or the Gnabgib, which is Big Bang backwards, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's what could have happened to the universe. But even if the universe's original expansion energy was so great that it avoids the Big Crunch, that's like an apple thrown at Earth's escape speed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's like the rockets that go to Mars someday, right? With people. Even then, you'd expect the universe to be slowing down with time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But we looked back through the history of the universe by looking at progressively more distant galaxies and by seeing that the evolution of this expansion rate is that in the first 9 billion years, yeah, it was slowing down. But in the last 5 billion years, it's been speeding up. So who asked for that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I think it's interesting to talk about a little bit of the human story of the Nobel Prize.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Which is, I mean, it's a really, first of all, the prize itself. It's kind of fascinating on the psychological level that prizes, I know we kind of think that prizes don't matter, but somehow they kind of focus the mind about some of the most special things we've accomplished.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The recognition, the funding, you know. And also inspiration for you. Like I said, when I was a little kid, they gave me the Nobel Prize. It inspires millions of young scientists. At the same time, there's a sadness to it a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I think that especially in the field, like depending on the field, but experimental fields that involve teams of, I don't know, sometimes hundreds of brilliant people, the Nobel Prize is only given to just a handful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Is it maxed at three?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. Yeah. And it's not even written in Alfred Nobel's will, it turns out. One of our teammates looked into it in a museum in Stockholm when we went there for Nobel week in 2011. The leaders who got the prize formally knew that without the rest of us working hard in the trenches, the result would not have been discovered.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So they invited us to participate in Nobel week. And so one of the team members looked in the will and it's not there. It's just tradition. It's archaic. That's the way science used to be done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it's not the way a lot of science is done now. And you look at gravitational wave discovery, which was recognized with the Nobel Prize in 2017, Ray Weiss at MIT got it and Kip Thorne and Barry Barish at Caltech. And Ron Drever, one of the masterminds had passed away earlier in the year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So again, one of the rules of Nobel is that it's not given posthumously, or at least the one exception might be if they've made their decision and they're busy making their press releases right before October, the first week in October or whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then the person passes away. I think they don't change their minds then. But yeah, it doesn't square with today's reality that a lot of science is done by big teams, in that case, a team of a thousand people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In our case, it was two teams consisting of about 50 people. And we used techniques that were arguably developed in part by people who, astrophysicists who weren't even on those two papers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, some of them were, but other papers were written by other people, you know, and so it's like we're standing on the shoulders of giants. And none of those people was officially recognized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And to me, it was okay. You know, again, it was the thrill of doing the work. And ultimately the work, the discovery was recognized with the prize. And, you know, we got to participate in Nobel week.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And, you know, it's okay with me. I've known other physicists whose lives were ruined because they did not get the Nobel Prize and they felt strongly that they should have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it doesn't- Ralph Alpher of the Alpher-Beta-Gamoff, you know, paper predicting the microwave background radiation. He should have gotten it. His advisor Gamoff was dead by that point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, you know, Penzias and Wilson got it for the discovery. And Alpher, apparently from colleagues who knew him well, I've talked to them, his life was ruined by this. He just, it just nodded at his innards so much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's very possible that in a small handful of people, even three, that you would be one of the Nobel, one of the winners of the Nobel Prize. That doesn't weigh heavy on you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, you know, there were the two team leaders, Saul Perlmutter and Brian Schmidt, and usually it's the team leaders that are recognized. And then Adam Rees was my postdoc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: First author, I guess.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, first author. I was second author of that paper. Yeah. So I was his direct mentor at the time, although he was, you know, one of these people who just, you know, runs with things. He was an MIT undergraduate, by the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Harvard graduate student and then a postdoc as a so-called Miller fellow for basic research and science at Berkeley, something that I was back in 84 to 86.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But you're, you know, you're largely a free agent, but he worked quite closely with me and he came to Berkeley to work with me and on Schmidt's team, he was charged with analyzing the data and he measured the brightnesses of these distant supernovae, showing that they're fainter and thus more distant than anticipated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that led to this conclusion that the universe had to have accelerated in order to push them out to such great distances. And I was shocked when he showed me the data, the results of his calculations and measurements.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But it's very, you know, so he deserved it. And on Saul's team, Gerson Goldhaber deserved it, but he died, I think a year earlier in 2010, but that would have been four.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so, and me, well, I was on both teams, but you know, was I number four, five, six, seven? I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's also very, so if I were to, it's possible that you're, I mean, I can make a very good case for you're in the three. And does that psychologically, I mean, listen, it weighs on me a little bit because I, I don't know what to do with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It, it, uh, perhaps it should motivate, uh, the rethinking like Time Magazine started doing like, you know, Person of the Year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And like they would, they would start doing like concepts and almost like the black hole gets the Nobel Prize or the Excellular Universe gets the Nobel Prize. And here's the list of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So like, or like the Oscar that you could say, because it's a team effort now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's a team. It should be redone. And the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics, which was started by Yuri Milner and Zuckerberg is involved in others as well. You know, uh, they recognize the larger team.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, they, they recognize teams. And so in fact, both teams in the accelerating universe were recognized with the Breakthrough Prize in 2015.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Nevertheless, the same three people, Reese, Perlmutter and Schmidt got the red carpet rolled out for them and were at the big ceremony and shared half of the prize money.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the rest of us, roughly 50, shared the other half and didn't get to go to the ceremony. So, but I, I feel for them. I mean, for the gravitational waves, it was a thousand people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What are they going to do? Invite everyone? For the Higgs particle, it was 68,000 physicists and engineers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In fact, because of the whole issue of who gets it experimentally, that discovery still has not been recognized, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The theoretical work by Peter Higgs and, uh, Angler got recognized, but there was a troika of other people who wrote, perhaps wrote the most complete paper and they were, they were left out and, um, another guy died, you know, and.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, it's hard. It's all of this heartbreaking. Some people argue that the Nobel Prize has been diluted to, because if you look at Roger Penrose, you can make an argument that he should get the prize by himself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Like, it's, so separate those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Could have and should have, perhaps he should have perhaps gotten it with Hawking before Hawking's death.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. Right. The problem was Hawking radiation had not been detected, but you could argue that Hawking made enough other fundamental contributions to the theoretical study of black holes and the observed data were already good enough at the time of.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Before Hawking's death. Okay. I mean, the latest results by Reinhard Genzel's group is that they see the time dilation effect of a star that's passing very close to the black hole in the middle of our galaxy. That's cool.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, and it adds additional evidence, but hardly anyone doubted the existence of the supermassive black hole and Andrea Gez's group, I believe hadn't yet shown that relativistic effect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And yet she got part of the prize as well. So clearly it was given for the, the original evidence that was really good. And that evidence is at least a decade old, you know, so one could make the case for Hawking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137
