body.input: One could make the case that in 2016, when Mayor and K. Lowes won the Nobel prize for the discovery of the first exoplanet, 51B Pegasi.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, there was a fellow at Penn State, Alex Woleshawn, who in 1992, three years preceding 1995, found a planet orbiting a pulsar, a very weird kind of star, a neutron star.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that wouldn't have been a normal planet. Sure. And so the Nobel committee, you know, they gave it for the discovery of planets around normal, sun-like stars, but, but hell, you know, Woleshawn found a planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So they could have given it to him as the third person instead of to Jim Peebles for the development of what's called physical cosmology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: He's at Princeton. He deserved it, but they could have given Nobel for the development of physical cosmology to Peebles. And I would claim some other people were pretty important in that development as well, you know, and they could have given it some other year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there's, there's a lot of controversy. I try not to dwell on it. Was I number three? Probably not. You know, Adam Reese did the work. You know, I helped bounce ideas off of him, but we wouldn't have had the result without him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah. And I was on both teams for reasons. I mean, you know, I, the, the style of the first team, the supernova cosmology project didn't match mine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They came largely from experimental high energy particle physics, physics, where there's these hierarchical teams and stuff. And it's hard for the little guy to, to have a say. At least that's what I kind of thought.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Whereas the team of astronomers led by Brian Schmidt was first of all, a bunch of my friends and they grew up as astronomers making contributions on little teams and we decided to band together, but all of us had our voices heard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it was sort of a, a culture, a style that I preferred really. But let me tell you a story at the Nobel banquet. Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I'm sitting there between two physicists who are, who are members of the committee of the Swedish national Academy of sciences. You know, and I strategically kept, you know, offering them wine and stuff during this long drawn out Nobel ceremony.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. And I got them to be pretty talkative. And then in a, in a polite diplomatic way, I started asking them pointed questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And basically they admitted that if there are four or more people equally deserving, they wait for one of them to die. Or they just don't give the prize at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: When it's unclear who the three are, at least unclear to them, but unclear to them it's they're not even right. Part of the time, I mean, Jocelyn Bell discovered pulsars with a radio antennas, a set of radio antennas that her advisor, Anthony Hewish.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Conceived and built, so he deserves some credit, but, but he didn't discover the pulsar. She did. And his initial reaction to the data that she showed him was a condescending rubbish, my dear. Yeah. I'm not kidding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now I know Jocelyn Bell and she did not let this destroy her life. She won every other prize under the sun. Okay. Vera Rubin, arguably one of the discoverers of dark matter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Although there, if you look at the history, there were a number of people, and that was the issue. I think there were a number of people, four or more, who had similar data and similar ideas at about the same time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Rubin won every prize under the sun. The new big large scale survey telescope being built in Chile is being renamed the Vera Rubin telescope, because she passed away in December of 2015, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, it'll conduct this survey, large scale survey with the Rubin telescope. So she's been recognized, but never with the Nobel prize. And I would say that to her credit, she did not let that consume her life either.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And perhaps it was a bit easier because there had been no Nobel given for the discovery of dark matter. Whereas in the case of pulsars and Jocelyn Bell, there was a prize given for the discovery of the freaking pulsars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And she didn't get it. What a travesty of justice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So I also think as a fan of fiction, as a fan of stories, that the travesty and the tragedy and the unfairness and the tension of it is what makes the prize and similar prizes beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The decisions of other humans that result in dreams being broken. And, you know, like that's why we love the Olympics. There's so many, you know, people athletes give their whole life for this particular moment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then there's referee decisions and like little slips of here and there, like the little misfortunes that destroy entire dreams. And that's, it's weird to say, but it feels like that makes the entirety of it even more special.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If it was perfect, it wouldn't be interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, humans like competition and they like heroes. And unfortunately it gives the impression to youngsters today that science is still done by white men with gray beards wearing white lab coats.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And I'm very pleased to see that this year, you know, Andrea Ghez, the fourth woman in the history of the physics prize to have received it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then two women, one at Berkeley, one elsewhere won the Nobel prize in chemistry without any male co-recipient.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so that's sending a message, I think, to girls that they can do science and they have role models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I think the breakthrough prize and other such prizes show that teams get recognized as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And if you pay attention to the newspapers, you know, most of the good authors like, you know, Dennis Overbye of the New York Times and others said that these were teams of people and they emphasize that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And, you know, they all played a role. And, you know, maybe if some grad student hadn't soldered some circuit, maybe the whole thing wouldn't have worked, you know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But still, you know, Ray Weiss, Kip Thorne was the theoretical, you know, impetus for the whole search for gravitational waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Barry Barish brought the MIT and Caltech teams together to get them to cooperate at a time when the project was nearly dead, from what I understand, and contributed greatly to the experimental setup as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: He's a great experimental physicist, but he was really good at bringing these two teams together instead of having them duke it out in blows and leaving both of them bleeding and dying.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You know, the National Science Foundation was going to cut the funding from what I understand, you know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So there's human drama involved in this whole thing. And the Olympics, yeah, you know, a runner, a swimmer, a runner, you know, they slip just at the moment they were taking off from the first thing and that cost them some fraction of a second and that's it. They didn't win, you know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And in that case, I mean, the coaches, the families, which I've met a lot of Olympic athletes, and the coaches and the families of the athletes are really the winners of the medals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But they don't get the medal. And it's, you know, credit assignment is a fascinating thing. I mean, that's the full human story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And outside of prizes, it's fascinating. I mean, just to be in the middle of it for artificial intelligence, there's a field of deep learning that's really exciting and people have been, there's yet another award, the Turing Award given for deep learning to three folks who are very much responsible for the field, but so are a lot of others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, that's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there's a few, there's a fellow by the name of Schmidt Huber who sort of symbolizes the forgotten folks in the deep learning community.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, you know, that's the unfortunate sad thing. We remember Isaac Newton, we remember these special figures and the ones that flew close to them we forget.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, that's right. And, you know, often the breakthroughs are made based on the body of knowledge that had been assimilated prior to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, you know, again, people like to worship heroes. You mentioned the Oscars earlier and, you know, you look at the direct, I mean, well, I mean, okay, directors and stuff sometimes get awards and stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But, you know, you look at even something like, I don't know, songwriters, musicians, Elton John or something, right? Bernie Taupin, right? Wrote many of the words or he's not as well known or the Beatles or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I was heartbroken to learn that Elvis didn't write most of his songs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, Elvis, that's right. There you go. But he was the king, right? And he had such a personality and he was such a performer. Right? But it's the unsung heroes in many cases. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So maybe taking a step back, we talked about the Nobel Prize for the Accelerating Universe, but your work and the ideas around supernova were important in detecting this accelerating universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Can we go to the very basics of what is this beautiful, mysterious object of a supernova?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. So a supernova is an exploding star. Most stars die a relatively quiet death, our own sun will, despite the fact that it'll become a red giant and incinerate Earth. It'll do that reasonably slowly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But there's a small minority of stars that end their lives in a titanic explosion. And that's not only exciting to watch from afar, but it's critical to our existence because it is in these explosions that the heavy elements synthesize through nuclear reactions during the normal course of the star's evolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And during the explosion itself, get ejected into the cosmos, making them available as raw material for new stars, planets, and ultimately life. And that's just a great story, the best in some ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So we like to study these things and our origins, but it turns out these are incredibly useful beacons as well, because if you know how powerful an exploding star really is by measuring the apparent brightness at its peak in galaxies whose distances we already know through having made other measurements,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: and you can thus calibrate how powerful the thing really is, and then you find ones that are much more distant, then you can use their observed brightness compared with their true intrinsic power or luminosity to judge their distance and hence the distance of the galaxy in which they're located.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's like looking at, let me just give this one analogy, you judge the distance of an oncoming car at night by looking at how bright its headlights appear to be, and you've calibrated how bright the headlights are of a car that's two or three meters away of known distance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you go, well, that's a faint headlight, and so that's pretty far away. You also use the apparent angular separation between the two headlights as a consistency check in your brain, but that's what your brain is doing. So we can do that for cars, we can do that for stars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Nice, I like that. But with cars, the headlights are all, there's some variation, but they're somewhat similar, so you can make those kinds of conclusions. How much variation is there between supernova that you can detect them?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Right. So first of all, there are several different ways that stars can explode, and it depends on their mass and whether they're in a binary system and things like that. And the ones that we used for these cosmological purposes studying the expansion of the history of the universe are the so-called type Roman numeral I, lowercase a, type Ia supernovae.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They come from a weird type of a star called a white dwarf. Our own sun will turn into a white dwarf in about seven billion years. It'll have about half its present mass compressed into a volume just the size of Earth. So that's an inordinate density.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Okay, it's incredibly dense. And the matter is what's called by quantum physicists degenerate matter, not because it's morally reprehensible or anything like that, but this is just the name that quantum physicists give to electrons that are squeezed into a very tight space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The electrons take on a motion due to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and also due to the Pauli exclusion principle that electrons don't like to be in the same place. They like to avoid each other. So those two things mean that a lot of electrons are moving very rapidly, which gives the star an extra pressure far above the thermal pressure associated with just the random motions of particles inside the star.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So it's a weird type of star, but normally it wouldn't explode and our sun won't explode, except that if such a white dwarf is in a pair with another more or less normal star, it can steal material from that normal star until it gets to an unstable limit, roughly one and a half times the mass of our sun, 1.4 or so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This is known as the Chandrasekhar limit after Subramanian Chandrasekhar, an Indian astrophysicist who figured this out when he was about 20 years old on a voyage from India to England where he was to be educated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And then he did this and then 50 years later, he won the Nobel Prize in physics in 1984 largely for this work that he did as a youngster who was on his way to be educated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh, and his advisor, the great Arthur Eddington in England, who had done a lot of great things and was a great astrophysicist, nevertheless, he too was human and had his faults.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: He ridiculed Chandra's scientific work at a conference in England and most of us, if we had been Chandra, would have just given up astrophysics at that time when the great Arthur Eddington ridicules our work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's another inspirational story for the youngster. Just keep going.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Ignore your advisors. Yeah, no matter what your advisor says. Or don't always pay attention to your advisor. Don't lose hope if you really think you're on to something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That doesn't mean never listen to your advisor. They may have sage advice as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But anyway, when a white dwarf grows to a certain mass, it becomes unstable. And one of the ways it can end its life is to go through a thermonuclear runaway. So basically, the carbon nuclei inside the white dwarf start fusing together to form heavier nuclei.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the energy that those fusion reactions emit doesn't go into being dissipated out of the star or whatever or expanding it the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If you take a blowtorch through the middle of the Sun, you heat up its gases, the gases would expand and cool. But this degenerate star can't expand and cool.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so the energy pumped in through these fusion reactions goes into making the nuclei move faster. And that gets more of them sufficiently close together that they can undergo nuclear fusion, thereby releasing more energy that goes into speeding up more nuclei.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And thus you have a runaway, a bomb, an uncontrolled fusion reactor, right? Instead of the controlled fusion, which is what our Sun does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Okay, our Sun is a marvelous controlled fusion reactor. This is what we need here on Earth, fusion energy to solve our energy crisis, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the Sun holds the stuff in through gravity and you need a big mass to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So this uncontrolled fusion reaction blows up a star that's pretty much the same in all cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And you measure it to be almost the same in all cases, but the devil is in the details. And in fact, we observe them to not be all the same.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And theoretically, they might not be all the same because the rate of the fusion reactions might depend on the amount of trace heavier elements in the white dwarf.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And that could depend on how old it is, whether it was born billions of years ago when there weren't many heavier elements or whether it's a relatively young white dwarf and all kinds of other things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And part of my work was to show that indeed not all the type 1A's are the same. You have to be careful when you use them. You have to calibrate them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They're not standard candles the way it just if all headlights or all candles were the same lumens or whatever, you'd say they're standard and then it would be relative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Standard candles is an awesome term. Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Standard candles is what astronomers like to say, but I don't like that term because there aren't any standard candles, but there are standardizable candles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And by looking at these type 1A's, you're calibrateable, standardizable, calibrateable. You look at enough of them in nearby galaxies whose distances you know independently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And what you can tell is that this is something that a colleague of mine, Mark Phillips, did who was on Schmidt's team and arguably was one of the people who deserved the Nobel Prize.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But he showed that the intrinsically more powerful type 1A's decline in brightness and it turns out rise in brightness as well more slowly than the less luminous 1A's.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so if you calibrate this by measuring a whole bunch of nearby ones and then you look at a distant one, instead of saying, well, it's a 100 watt type 1A supernova, they're much more powerful than that, by the way, plus or minus 50,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: you can say, no, it's 112 plus or minus 15 or it's 84 plus or minus 17.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It tells you where it is in the power scale and it greatly decreases the uncertainties. And that's what makes these things cosmologically useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I showed that if you spread the light out into a spectrum, you can tell spectroscopically that these things are different as well. And in 1991, I happened to study two of the extreme peculiar ones, the low luminosity ones and the high luminosity ones,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: 1991BG and 1991T. This showed that not all the 1A's are the same. And indeed, at the time of 1991, I was a little bit skeptical that we could use type 1A's because of this diversity that I was observing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But in 1993, Mark Phillips wrote a paper that showed this correlation between the light curve, the brightness versus time and the peak luminosity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Which gives you enough information to calibrate. Yeah, then they become calibrateable and that was a game changer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: How many type 1A's are out there to use for data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Now there are thousands of them. But at the time, the high Z team had 16 and the supernova cosmology project had 40. But the 16 were better measured than the 40. And so our statistical uncertainties were comparable if you look at the two papers that were published.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: How does that make you feel that there's these gigantic explosions just sprinkled out there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, I certainly don't want one to be very nearby and it would have to be within something like 10 light years to be an existential threat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So they can happen in our galaxy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh yeah, yeah. So they would be okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In most cases, we'd be okay because our galaxy is a hundred thousand light years across and you'd need one of these things to be within about 10 light years to be an existential threat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it gives birth to a bunch of other stars, I guess?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah, it gives birth to expanding gases that are chemically enriched and those expanding gases mixed with other chemically enriched expanding gases or primordial clouds of hydrogen and helium.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, this is in a sense the greatest story ever told, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I teach this introductory astronomy course at Berkeley and I tell them there's only five or six things that I want them to really understand and remember.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And I'm going to come to their deathbed and I'm going to ask them about this. And if they get it wrong, I will retroactively fail.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Their whole career will have been shot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That's a student's worst nightmare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't want to observe a total solar eclipse and yet they had the opportunity to do so. I will retroactively fail them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But one of them is, where did we come from? Where did the elements in our DNA come from?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The carbon in our cells, the oxygen that we breathe, the calcium in our bones, the iron in our red blood cells, those elements, the phosphorus in our DNA, they all came from stars, from nuclear reactions in stars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And they were ejected into the cosmos and in some cases like iron made during the explosions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And those gases drifted out, mixed with other clouds, made a new star or a star cluster, some of whose members then evolved and exploded, thus enriching the gases in the galaxy progressively more with time until finally four and a half billion years ago

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: from one of these chemically enriched clouds, our solar system formed with a rocky, Earth-like planet and somewhere, somehow, these self-replicating evolving molecules, bacteria formed and evolved through paramecia and amoebas and slugs and apes and us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And here we are, sentient beings that can ask these questions about our very origins and with our intellect and with the machines we make, come to a reasonable understanding of our origins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: What a beautiful story. I mean, if that does not put you at least in awe, if not in love with science and its power of deduction, I don't know what will, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's one of the greatest stories, if not the greatest story. Obviously, that's, you know, personality dependent and all that. It's a subjective opinion, but it's perhaps the greatest story ever told.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I mean, you could link it to the Big Bang and go even farther, right, to make an even more complete story. But as a subset, that's even in some ways a greater story than even the existence of the universe in some ways, because you could just imagine some really boring universe that never leads to sentient creatures such as ourselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And is a supernova usually the introduction to that story?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So are they usually the thing that launches the, is there other engines of creation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, the supernova is the one, I mean, I touch upon the subject earlier in my course, in fact, right about now in my lectures, because I talk about how our Sun right now is fusing hydrogen to form helium nuclei.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And later it'll form carbon and oxygen nuclei, but that's where the process will stop for our Sun. It's not massive enough. Some stars can, that are more massive, can go somewhat beyond that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So that's the beginning of, right, this idea of the birth of the heavy elements since they couldn't have been born at the time of the Big Bang. Conditions of temperature and pressure weren't sufficient to make any significant quantities of the heavier elements.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so, so that's the beginning, but then you need some of these stars to explode, right? Because if those heavy elements remained forever trapped in the cores of stars, then they would not be available for the production of new stars, planets, and ultimately life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So indeed the supernova, my main area of interest plays a leading role in this whole story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I saw that you got a chance to call Richard Feynman a mentor of yours when you were at Caltech. Do you have any fond memories of Feynman, any lessons that stick with you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Oh yeah. He was quite a character and one of the deepest thinkers of all time probably. And at least in my life, the physicist who had the single most intuitive understanding of how nature works, of anyone I've met,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I learned a number of things from him. He was not my thesis advisor. I worked with Wallace Sargent at Caltech on what are called active galaxies, big black holes in the centers of galaxies that are accreting or swallowing material, a little bit like the stuff of this year's Nobel Prize in Physics 2020.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But Feynman I had for two courses. One was general theory of relativity at the graduate level and one was applications of quantum physics to all kinds of interesting things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And he had this very intuitive way of looking at things that he tried to bring to his students. And he felt that if you can't explain something in a reasonably simple way to a non-scientist or at least someone who is versed a little bit with science but is not a professional scientist,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: then you probably don't understand it very well yourself, very thoroughly. So that in me made a desire to be able to explain science to the general public.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And I've often found that in explaining things, yeah, there's a certain part that I didn't really understand myself. That's one reason I like to teach the introductory courses to the lay public is that I sometimes find that my explanations are lacking in my own mind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So he did that for me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Is there, if I could just pause for a second, you said he had one of the most intuitive understandings of nature. If you could break apart what intuitive means, is that on a philosophical level?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: No, sort of physical. How do you draw a mental picture or a picture on paper of what's going on? And he's perhaps most famous in this regard for his Feynman diagrams, which in what's called quantum electrodynamics, a quantum field theory of electricity and magnetism,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: what you have are actually an exchange of photons between charged particles. And they might even be virtual photons if the particles are at rest relative to one another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And there are ways of doing calculations that are brute force that take pages on pages and pages of calculations. And Julian Schwinger developed some of the mathematics for that and won the Nobel Prize for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But Feynman had these diagrams that he made and he had a set of rules of what to do at the vertex. You'd have two particles coming together and then a particle going out and then two particles coming out again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And he'd have these rules associated when there were vertices and when there were particles splitting off from one another and all that. And it looked a little bit like a bunch of a hodgepodge at first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But to those who learned the rules and understood them, they saw that you could do these complex calculations in a much simpler way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And indeed, in some ways, Freeman Dyson had an even better knack for explaining really what quantum electrodynamics actually was. But I didn't know Freeman Dyson. I knew Feynman.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe he did have a more intuitive view of the world than Feynman did. But of the people I knew, Feynman was the most intuitive, most sort of, is there a picture? Is there a simple way you can understand this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And in the path that a particle follows even, you can figure out the, you can get the classical path, at least for a baseball or something like that, by using quantum physics if you want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But in a sense, the baseball sniffs out all possible paths. It goes out to the Andromeda galaxy and then goes to the batter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But the probability of doing that is very, very small because tiny little paths next door to any given path cancel out that path.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And the ones that all add together, they are the ones that are more likely to be followed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And this actually ties in with Fermat's principle of least action. And there are ideas in optics that go into this as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And it just sort of beautifully brings everything together. But the particle sniffs out all possible paths. What a crazy idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But if you do the mathematics associated with that, it ends up being actually useful, a useful way of looking at the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So you're also, I mean, you're widely acknowledged as, I mean, outside of your science work as being one of the greatest educators in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And Feynman is famous for being that. Is there something about being a teacher that you...

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, it's very, very rewarding when you have students who are really into it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And going back to Feynman at Caltech, I was taking these graduate courses and there were two of us, myself and Jeff Richmond,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: who's now a professor of physics at University of California, Santa Barbara, who asked lots of questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And a lot of the Caltech students are nervous about asking questions. They want to save face.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They seem to think that if they ask a question, their peers might think it's a stupid question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Well, I didn't really care what people thought and Jeff Richmond didn't either. And we ask all these questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And in fact, in many cases, they were quite good questions. And Feynman said, well, the rest of you should be having questions like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And I remember one time in particular when he said to the rest of the class, why is it always these two?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Aren't the rest of you curious about what I'm saying? Do you really understand it all that well?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: If so, why aren't you asking the next most logical question? No, you guys are too scared to ask these questions that these two are asking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: So he actually invited us to lunch a couple of times where just the three of us sat and had lunch with one of the greatest thinkers of 20th century physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And so, yeah, he rubbed off on me. So you encourage questions as well?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I encourage questions. Yeah, definitely. I mean, I encourage questions. I like it when students ask questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I tell them that they shouldn't feel shy about asking a question. Probably half the students in the class would have that same question if they even understood the material enough to ask that question. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Curiosity is the first step of seeing the beauty of something. And the question is the ultimate form of curiosity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Let me ask, what is the meaning of life?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The meaning of life, you know. From a cosmologist perspective or from a human perspective. Or from my personal, you know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Life is what you make of it really, right? It's, each of us has to have our own meaning. And it doesn't have to be, well, I think that in many cases meaning is to some degree associated with goals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You set some goals or expectations for yourself, things you want to accomplish, things you want to do, things you want to experience. And to the degree that you experience those and do those things, it can give you meaning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You don't have to change the world the way Newton or Michelangelo or Da Vinci did. I mean, people often say, change the world. But look, come on, there's seven and a half, close to eight billion of us now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Most of us are not going to change the world. And does that mean that most of us are leading meaningful lives? No. It just has to be something that gives you meaning, that gives you satisfaction, that gives you a good feeling about what you did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: And often, based on human nature, which can be very good and also very bad, but often it's the things that help others, that give us meaning and a feeling of satisfaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You taught someone to read, you cared for someone who was terminally ill, you brought up a nice family, you brought up your kids, you did a good job, you put your heart and soul into it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You read a lot of books, if that's what you wanted to do, had a lot of perspectives on life, you traveled the world, if that's what you wanted to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: But if some of these things are not within reach, you're in a socioeconomic position where you can't travel the world or whatever, you find other forms of meaning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It doesn't have to be some profound, I'm going to change the world, I'm going to be the one who everyone remembers type thing, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: In the context of the greatest story ever told, like the fact that we came from stars and now we're two apes asking about the meaning of life, how does that fit together?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Does that make any sense?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It does, it does, and this is sort of what I was referring to, that it's a beautiful universe that allows us to come into creation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's a way that the universe found of knowing, of understanding itself, because I don't think that inanimate rocks and stars and black holes and things have any real capability of abstract thoughts and of learning about the rest of the universe or even their origins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: They're just a pile of atoms that has no conscience, has no ability to think, has no ability to explore, and we do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I'm not saying we're the epitome of all life forever, but at least for life on Earth so far, the evidence suggests that we are the epitome in terms of the richness of our thoughts, the degree to which we can explore the universe, do experiments, build machines, understand our origins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I just hope that we use science for good, not evil, and that we don't end up destroying ourselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: The whales and dolphins are plenty intelligent. They don't ask abstract questions, they don't read books, but on the other hand, they're not in any danger of destroying themselves and everything else as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Maybe that's a better form of intelligence, but at least in terms of our ability to explore and make use of our minds, to me, it's this that gives me the potential for meaning, the fact that I can understand and explore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's kind of fascinating to think that the universe created us, and eventually we've built telescopes to look back at its origins and to wonder how the heck the thing works.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It's magnificent. It needn't have been that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: This is one of the multiverse things. You can alter the laws of physics or even the constants of nature, seemingly inconsequential things like the mass ratio of the proton and the neutron.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: Wake me up when it's over, right? What could be more boring?

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: It turns out you play with things a little bit like the ratio of the mass of the neutron to the proton, and you generally get boring universes, only hydrogen or only helium or only iron.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: You don't even get the rich periodic table, let alone bacteria, paramecia, slugs, and humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I'm not even anthropocentrizing this to the degree that I could. Even a rich periodic table wouldn't be possible if certain constants weren't this way, but they are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: That, to me, leads to the idea of a multiverse, that the dice were thrown many, many times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There's this cosmic archipelago where most of the universes are boring, and some might be more interesting,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: but we are in the rare breed that's really quite darn interesting. If there were only one, and maybe there is only one, well then that's truly amazing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We're lucky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: We're lucky, but I actually think there are lots in loss. Just like there are lots of planets, Earth isn't special for any particular reason.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: There are lots of planets in our solar system and especially around other stars, and occasionally there are going to be ones that are conducive to the development of complexity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: culminating in life as we know it. That's a beautiful story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137

body.input: I don't think there's a better way to end it, Alex. It's a huge honor. One of my favorite conversations I've had in this podcast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Alex Filippenko: Supernovae, Dark Energy, Aliens & the Expanding Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #137
