metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And it's kind of like that's sort of the business we're in. And in a sense with some of these ideas

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: in science, I feel a little bit the same way that there are some of these things where some things

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: like, for example, this whole idea... Well, so to relate to another sort of piece of history on the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: future, I mentioned at the beginning kind of complexity as this thing that I was interested

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: in back 40 years ago and so on. Where does complexity come from? Well, I think we kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: of nailed that. The answer is in the computational universe, even simple programs make it. And that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: kind of the secret that nature has that allows you to make it. So that's that part. But the bigger

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: picture there was this idea of this kind of computational paradigm, the idea that you could

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: go beyond mathematical equations, which had been sort of the primary modeling medium for 300 years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And so it was like, look, it is inexorably the case that people will use programs rather than

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: just equations. And I was saying that in the 1980s and people were... I published my big book,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: New Kind of Science, that'll be 20 years ago next year, so in 2002. And people are saying,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: oh no, this can't possibly be true. We know for 300 years we've been doing all this stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: To be fair, I now realize a little bit more analysis of what people actually said. In pretty

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: much every field other than physics, people said, oh, these are new models. That's pretty interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: In physics, people were like, we've got our physics models. We're very happy with them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Yeah, in physics, there's more resistance because of the attachment and the power of the equations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: the idea that programs might be the right way to approach this field. Was there some resistance?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And like you're saying, it takes time. For somebody who likes the idea of time dilation

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: and all these applications, I thought you would understand this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Yeah, right. And computational irreducibility as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: But it is really interesting that just 20 years, the span of 20 years, it's gone from pitchforks

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: and horror to, yeah, we get it. And it's helped that in our current effort in fundamental physics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: we've gotten a lot further and we've managed to put a lot of puzzle pieces together that make sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: But the thing that I've been thinking about recently is this field of complexity. So I

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: was a field builder back in the 1980s. I was like, okay, I'd understood this point that there was

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: this fundamental phenomenon of complexity and it showed up in lots of places. And I was like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: this is an interesting field of science. And I recently was reminded, I was at the very first

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: get together of what became the Santa Fe Institute. And I was like, in fact, there's even an audio

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: recording of me saying, people have been talking about, oh, what should this outfit do? And I was

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: saying, well, there is this thing that I've been thinking about. It's this idea of complexity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Nice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And it's like, and that's what that ended up-

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And you planted the seed of complexity at Santa Fe. That's beautiful. It's a beautiful vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: But I mean, so what's happened then is this idea of complexity. And I started the first

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: research center at University of Illinois for doing that in the first journal,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: complex systems and so on. And it's kind of an interesting thing in my life, at least,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: that it's kind of like you plant the seed, you have this idea, it's a kind of a science idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: You have this idea of sort of focusing on the phenomenon of complexity. The deeper idea was

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: this computational paradigm. But the nominal idea is this kind of idea of complexity. Okay. Then you

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: roll time forward 30 years or whatever, 35 years, whatever it is, and you say, what happened? Okay,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: well, now there are a thousand complexity institutes around the world, I think, more or less.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: We've been trying to count them. And there are 40 complexity journals, I think. And so

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: it's kind of like what actually happened in this field. And I look at a lot of what happened and

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: I have to admit, there's some eye rolling, so to speak, because it's kind of like, what's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: actually going on? Well, what people definitely got was this idea of computational models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And then they got, but they thought one of the kind of cognitive mistakes, I think, is they say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: we've got a computational model and we're looking at a system that's complex. And our computational

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: model gives complexity. By golly, that must mean it's right. And unfortunately, because complexity

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: is a generic phenomenon and computational irreducibility is a generic phenomenon that

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: actually tells you nothing. And so then the question is, well, what can you do? There's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: lot of things that have been done under this banner of complexity. And I think it's been very

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: successful in providing an interdisciplinary way of connecting different fields together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Yeah, which is powerful in itself. I mean, that's a very useful-

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: I mean, that's a very useful-

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Organizing, yeah, it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Right. It's a good organizing principle. But in the end, a lot of that is around this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: computational paradigm, computational modeling. That's the raw material that powers that kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: correspondence, I think. But the question is, what is the- I was just thinking recently,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: for years, people have told me, you should start some Wolfram Institute that does basic science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: All I have is a company that builds software and we have a little piece that does basic science as

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: kind of a hobby. People are saying, you should start this Wolfram Institute thing. And I've been,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: because I've known about lots of institutes and I've seen kind of their flow of money and

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: and kind of what happens in different situations and so on. So I've been kind of reluctant, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: I have realized that what we've done with our company over the last 35 years, we built a very

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: good machine for doing R&D and innovating and creating things. And I just applied that machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: to the physics project. That's how we did the physics project in a fairly short amount of time

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: with an efficient machine with various people involved and so on. And so it works for basic

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: science and it's like, we can do more of this. And so-

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And biology and chemistry, it's become an institute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Yes. Well, it needs to become an institute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: An official institute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Right. But the thing that I was thinking about, okay, so what do we do with complexity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: There are all these people who've- what should happen to that field?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Yeah. And what I realized is there's kind of this area of foundations of complexity

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: that's about these questions about simple programs, what they do, that's far away from

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: a bunch of the detailed applications that people- well, it's not far away. It's the under,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: the bedrock underneath those applications. And so I realized recently, this is my recent kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: little innovation of a sort, a post that I'll do very soon, about the foundations of complexity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: what really are they? I think there are really two ideas, two conceptual ideas that I hadn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: really enunciated, I think, before. One is what I call meta-modeling, the other is rulliology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: So what is meta-modeling? So meta-modeling is you've got this complicated model and it's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: model of hedgehogs interacting with this, interacting with that. And the question is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: what's really underneath that? What is it? Is it a Turing machine? Is it a cellular automaton?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: What is the underlying stuff underneath that model? And so there's this kind of meta-science

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: question of, given these models, what is the core model? And I realized, I mean, to me,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: that's sort of an obvious question, but then I realized I've been doing language design for 40

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: years and language design is exactly that question. Underneath all of this detailed stuff people do,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: what are the underlying primitives? And that's a question people haven't tended to ask about

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: models. They say, well, we've got this nice model for this and that and the other, what's really

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: underneath it? Because once you have the thing that's underneath it, well, for example, this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: multi-computation idea is an ultimate meta-modeling idea because it's saying underneath all these

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: fields is one kind of paradigmatic structure. And you can imagine the same kind of thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: much sort of shallower levels in different kinds of modeling. So the first activity is this kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: meta-modeling, the kind of the models about models, so to speak. What's drilling down into models?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: That's one thing. The other thing is this thing that I think we're going to call ruleology,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: which is kind of the, okay, you've got these simple rules. You've got cellular automata,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: you've got Turing machines, you've got substitution systems, you've got register machines,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: you've got all these different things. What do they actually do in the wild? And this is an area

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: that I've spent a lot of time working on. And it's a lot of stuff in my new kind of science book is

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: about this. This new book I wrote about combinators is full of stuff like this. And this journal,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Complex Systems, has lots of papers about these kinds of things. But there isn't really a home

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: for people who do ruleology or what I'm not- It's the, as you call it, the basic science of rules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: Yes. Yes, right. So it's like you've got some, what is it? Is it mathematics? No,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: it isn't really like mathematics. In fact, from my now understanding of meta-mathematics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: I understand that it's the molecular dynamics level. It's not the level that mathematicians

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: have traditionally cared about. It's not computer science because computer science is about writing

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: programs that do things that were for a purpose, not programs in the wild, so to speak. It's not

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: physics. It doesn't have anything to do with, it may be underneath some physics, but it's not physics

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: as such. So it just hasn't had a home. And if you look at, but what's great about it is it's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: surviving field, so to speak. It's something where one of the things I find sort of inspiring

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: about mathematics, for example, is you look at mathematics that was done in ancient Greece,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: ancient Babylon, Egypt, and so on. It's still here today. You find an icosahedron that somebody made

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: in ancient Egypt. You look at it, oh, that's a very modern thing. It's an icosahedron. It's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: timeless kind of activity. And this idea of studying simple rules and what they do,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: it's a timeless activity. And I can see that over the last 40 years or so, as even with cellular

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: automata, it's kind of like you can sort of catalog what are the different cellular automata used for

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: and the simplest rules, like one, you might even know this one, rule 184. Rule 184 is a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: minimal model for road traffic flow. And it's also a minimal model for various other things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: But it's kind of fun that you can literally say rule 90 is a minimal model for this and this and

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: this. Rule four is a minimal model for this. And it's kind of remarkable that you can just buy in

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: this raw level of this kind of study of rules, they then branch, they're the raw material that

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: you can use to make models of different things. So it's a very pure basic science, but it's one

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: that people have explored it, but they've been kind of a little bit in the wilderness. And I think

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: one of the things that I would like to do finally is I always thought that sort of this notion of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: pure NKS, pure NKS being the acronym for my book, New Kind of Science, was something that people

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: should be doing. And we tried to figure out what's the right institutional structure to do this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: stuff. We dealt with a bunch of universities, oh, can we do this here? Well, what department

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: would it be in? Well, it isn't in a department, it's its own new kind of thing. That's why the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: book was called The New Kind of Science, because that's an increasingly good description of what

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: it is, so to speak. We were thinking about kind of the ruleological society, because we're realizing

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: that it's kind of... I love it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: It's very interesting. I mean, I've never really done something like this before, because there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: this whole group of researchers who've been doing things that are really, in some cases, very

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: elegant, very surviving, very solid, here's this thing that happens in this very abstract system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: But it's like, what is that part of? It doesn't have a home. And I think that's something I kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: of fault myself for not having been more... When complexity was developing in the 80s,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: I didn't understand the danger of applications. That is, it's really cool that you can apply this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: to economics, and you can apply it to evolutionary biology, and this and that and the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: But what happens with applications is everything gets sucked into the applications. And the pure

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: stuff, it's like the pure mathematics. There isn't any pure mathematics, so to speak. It's all just

body.input: applications of mathematics. And I failed to kind of make sure that this kind of pure area was kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: of maintained and developed. And I think now, one of the things I want to try to do, and it's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: funny thing, because I'm used to... Look, I've been a tech CEO for more than half my life now. So

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: so this is what I know how to do. And I can make stuff happen and get projects to happen,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: even as it turns out basic science projects in that kind of setting, and how that translates into...

body.input: There are a lot of people working on, for example, our physics project distributed through

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: the academic world, and that's working just great. But the question is, can we have a sort

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: of accelerator mechanism that makes use of what we've learned in R&D innovation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: And but on the other hand, it's a funny thing because in a company, in the end, the thing is...

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: It's a company. It makes products that sells things to people. When you're doing basic research,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234

body.input: one of the challenges is there isn't that same kind of sort of mechanism. And so it's how do you

body.input: The following is a conversation with Barry Barish, a theoretical physicist at Caltech

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: and the observation of gravitational waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: LIGO, or the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory, is probably the most precise

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: measurement device ever built by humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It consists of two detectors with 4 kilometer long vacuum chambers situated 3,000 kilometers

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: apart, operating in unison to measure a motion that is 10,000 times smaller than the width

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: of a proton.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It is the smallest measurement ever attempted by science, a measurement of gravitational

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: waves caused by the most violent and cataclysmic events in the universe, occurring over tens

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: of millions of light years away.

body.input: You've mentioned that you were always curious about the physical world and that an early

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: question you remember stood out where you asked your dad, why does ice float on water?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And he couldn't answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And this was very surprising to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So you went on to learn why.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Maybe you can speak to what are some early questions in math and physics that really

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: sparked your curiosity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Yeah, that memory is kind of something I used to illustrate something I think that's common

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: in science, is that people that do science somehow have maintained something that kids

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: always have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: A small kid, eight years old or so, asks you so many questions usually, typically that

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: you consider them pests, you tell them to stop asking so many questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And somehow our system manages to kill that in most people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So in school we make people to study and do their things, but not to pester them by asking

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: too many questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And I think not just myself, but I think it's typical of scientists like myself that have

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: somehow escaped that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Maybe we're still children or maybe we somehow didn't get it beaten out of us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But I think it's, I teach it in college level and it's to me, one of the biggest deficits

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: is the lack of curiosity if you want that we've beaten out of them because I think it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: an innate human quality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Is there some advice or insights you can give to how to keep that flame of curiosity going?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: I think it's a problem of both parents and the parents should realize that's a great

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: quality we have, that you're curious and that's good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Instead we have expressions like curiosity killed the cat and more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But I mean, basically it's not thought to be a good thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Curiosity killed the cat means if you're too curious you get in trouble.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: I don't like cats anyway, so maybe it's a good thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That to me needs to be solved really in education and in homes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's a realization that there's certain human qualities that we should try to build

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: on and not destroy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: One of them is curiosity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Anyway, back to me and curiosity, I was a pest and asked a lot of questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: My father generally could answer them at that age.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: basically that ice is made out of water.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Why does it float on water?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He couldn't answer it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It may not have been the first question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's the first one that I remember.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That was the first time that I realized that to learn and answer your own curiosity or

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: questions, there's various mechanisms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But eventually you do it by what we call research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But it's driven by if you're hopefully you ask good questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: If you ask good questions and you have the mechanisms to solve them, then you do what

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: I do in life, basically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Not necessarily physics, but it's a great quality in humans and we should nurture it.

body.input: Do you remember any other kind of in high school, maybe early college, more basic physics

body.input: That's one of the big questions.

body.input: So we even know less in a sense, the more we look.

body.input: So of course, I think that's one of the areas that almost it's universal.

body.input: our recent, their last 20, 30 years, certainly dark energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And he wrote down not only just the theory, a theory, but a theory that lasted decades

body.input: and has only been improved on of beta decay, that is the radiation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And you might recall in electromagnetism, we make electromagnetic waves in a simple

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: You take a plus charge and minus charge, you oscillate like this, and that makes electromagnetic

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And a physicist named Hertz made a receiver that could detect the waves and put it in

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: the next room.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He saw them and moved forward and backward and saw that it was wave-like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So Einstein said it won't be a dipole like that, it'll be a four-pole thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And that's what it's called a quadrupole moment that gives the gravitational wave.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So that again, by insight, not by derivation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That's at the table for which he needed to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: At the same time, in the same year, Schwarzschild, not Einstein, said there were things called

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: black holes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So it's interesting that that came the same.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So what year was that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213
Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It was in parallel with, I should probably know this, but did Einstein not have any intuition

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: that there should be such things as black holes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That came from Schwarzschild.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Oh, interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So Schwarzschild, who was a German theoretical physicist, he got killed in the war, I think,

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: in the First World War, two years later or so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He's the one that proposed black holes, that there were black holes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It feels like a natural conclusion of general relativity, no?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Or is that not?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Well, it may seem like it, but I don't know about a natural conclusion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's a result of curved space-time, though.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But it's such a weird result that you might have to...

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's a special...

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Yeah, it's a special case.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Interestingly, Einstein then, an interesting part of the story is that Einstein then left

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: the problem, most physicists, because it really wasn't derived.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He just didn't pick up on it or general relativity much because quantum mechanics became the

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: thing in physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And Einstein only picked up this problem again after he immigrated to the US.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So he came to the US in 1932, and I think in 1935, he was working with another physicist

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: called Rosen, who he did several important works with, and they revisited the question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And they had a problem that most of us as students always had, that studied general

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: relativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: General relativity is really hard because it's four-dimensional instead of three-dimensional.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And if you don't set it up right, you get infinities, which don't belong there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: We call them coordinate singularities as a name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But if you get these infinities, you don't get the answers you want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And he was trying to derive now general relativity from general relativity, gravitational waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And in doing it, he kept getting these infinities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And so he wrote a paper with Rosen that he submitted to our most important journal, Physical

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Review Letters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And when it was submitted to Physical Review Letters, it was entitled, Do Gravitational

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Waves Exist?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: A very funny title to write 20 years after he proposed they exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But it's because he had found these singularities, these infinities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And so the editor at that time, and part of it that I don't know is peer review.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: We live and die by peer review as scientists send our stuff out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: We don't know when peer review actually started or what peer review Einstein ever experienced

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: before this time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But the editor of Physical Review sent this out for review.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He had a choice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He could take any article and just accept it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He could reject it or he could send it for review.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: I believe the editors used to have much more power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And he was a young man.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: His name was Tate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And he ended up being editor for years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So he sent this for review to a theoretical physicist named Robertson, who was also in

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: this field of general relativity, who happened to be on sabbatical at that moment at Caltech.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Otherwise his institution was Princeton where Einstein was.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And he saw that the way they set up the problem, the infinities were like I make it as a student.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Because if you don't set it up right in general relativity, you get these infinities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And so he reviewed the article and gave an illustration that if they set it up in what

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: are called cylindrical coordinates, these infinities went away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: The editor of physical review was obviously intimidated by Einstein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: He wrote this really not a letter back like I would get saying, you're screwed up in your

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: paper instead.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It was kind of what do you think of the comments of our...

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Einstein wrote back.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's a well-documented letter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Wrote back a letter to physical review saying, I didn't send you the paper to send it to

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: one of your so-called experts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: I sent it to you to publish.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: I withdraw the paper and he never published again in that journal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That was 1936.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Instead he rewrote it with the fixes that were made, changed the title and published

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: it in what was called the Franklin Review, which is the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia,

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: which is Benjamin Franklin Institute, which doesn't have a journal now, but did at that

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So the article is published.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's the last time he ever wrote about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It remained controversial.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So it wasn't until close to 1960, 1958, where there was a conference that brought together

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: the experts in general relativity to try to sort out whether it was true that there were

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: gravitational waves or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: There was a very nice derivation by a British theorist from the heart of the theory that

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: gets gravitational waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That was number one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: The second thing that happened at that meeting is Richard Feynman was there and Feynman said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: well, if there's a typical Feynman, if there's gravitational waves, they need to be able

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: to do something, otherwise they don't exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So they have to be able to transfer energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So he made an idea of a Gidankan experiment that is just a bar with a couple of rings

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And then if a gravitational wave goes through it, it distorts the bar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And that creates friction on these little rings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And that's heat and that's energy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So that meant- Is that a good idea?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That sounds like a good idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It means that he showed that with the distortion of space-time, you could transfer energy just

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: by this little idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And it was shown theoretically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So at that point, it was believed theoretically then by people that gravitational waves should

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: No, we should be able to detect them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: We should be able to detect them except that they're very, very small.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So there's a bunch of questions here, but what kind of events would generate gravitational

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: waves?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: You have to have this, what I call quadruple moment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That comes about if I have, for example, two objects that go around each other like this,

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: like the earth around the sun or the moon around the earth, or in our case, it turns

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: out to be two black holes going around each other like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So how's that different than basic oscillation back and forth?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Is it just more common in nature to have- Oscillation is a dipole moment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So it has to be in three-dimensional space kind of oscillation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So you have to have something that's three-dimensional that'll give what I called a quadruple moment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: That's just built into this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And luckily in nature, you have stuff out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And luckily things exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And it is luckily because the effect is so small that you could say, look, I can take

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: a barbell and spin it, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: And detect the gravitational waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But unfortunately, no matter how much I spin it, how fast I spin it, so I know how to make

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: gravitational waves, but they're so weak, I can't detect them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So we have to take something that's stronger than I can make.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Otherwise we would do what Hertz did for electromagnetic waves, go in our lab, take a barbell.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Put it on something, spin it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Can I ask a dumb question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So a single object that's weirdly shaped, does that generate gravitational waves?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So if it's rotating?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: But it's just much weaker signal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It's weaker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Well, we didn't know what the strongest signal would be that we would see.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: We targeted seeing something called neutron stars actually, because black holes we don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: know very much about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: It turned out we were a little bit lucky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: There was a stronger source, which was the black holes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: Well, another ridiculous question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: So you say waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213

body.input: What does a wave mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Barry Barish: Gravitational Waves and the Most Precise Device Ever Built | Lex Fridman Podcast #213
